subjects.name: Physics
assessmentObjectives: AO1 Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of facts, concepts, and terminology
AO2 Apply and use knowledge and understanding in familiar and unfamiliar situations
AO3 Construct, analyse and evaluate hypotheses, research questions, methodologies, and results
AO4 Demonstrate the ability to solve problems, including those requiring quantitative skills

topics.title: Space, time and motion
topics.syllabusDescription: Kinematics, forces and momentum, work, energy and power, rigid body mechanics, and Galilean and special relativity. Covers the mathematical description and analysis of motion in classical and relativistic frameworks.

subtopics.title: Kinematics
subtopics.syllabusContent: Motion described in terms of position, velocity and acceleration. Equations of uniform acceleration, projectile motion in the absence of fluid resistance, and qualitative effects of fluid resistance on projectiles including terminal speed.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Projectile motion quantitatively limited to no fluid resistance. Parabolic trajectory understood conceptually but equation not required. Familiarity with projectiles launched horizontally, above and below horizontal. Constant g near Earth's surface only. Fluid resistance refers to gases and liquids.
coreConcepts: Displacement is a vector change in position; distance is the scalar total path length — they are equal only for straight-line motion in one direction.
Velocity is the rate of change of displacement (Δx/Δt); speed is the magnitude of velocity and is always non-negative.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity; a body can be decelerating yet have positive acceleration depending on direction convention.
The four suvat equations (v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as, s = (u+v)/2 · t) apply only under constant acceleration.
Projectile motion is resolved into independent horizontal (constant velocity) and vertical (constant acceleration g) components.
Fluid resistance introduces a velocity-dependent retarding force, making acceleration non-uniform and creating a terminal speed where net force is zero.
Instantaneous values are found from the gradient of a displacement-time or velocity-time graph; average values use total change over total time.
The trajectory of a projectile without fluid resistance is parabolic due to the combination of constant horizontal velocity and uniformly accelerated vertical motion.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming displacement and distance are always equal — they differ whenever the path is curved or direction reverses.
Treating the suvat equations as applicable to non-uniform acceleration — they require constant acceleration only.
Believing a body thrown horizontally has zero initial vertical velocity — it does; only the horizontal component is non-zero initially.
Confusing the direction of acceleration with the direction of motion — a ball thrown upward has downward acceleration throughout its flight.
Thinking terminal velocity means zero velocity — it means zero acceleration (constant, non-zero velocity).
Assuming fluid resistance reduces only the range of a projectile — it also reduces height, time of flight and changes trajectory from parabolic.
Believing that heavier objects always fall faster — in the absence of fluid resistance all objects accelerate at g regardless of mass.

conceptual: Explain why a projectile launched at 45° achieves maximum range in the absence of fluid resistance.
Describe how fluid resistance changes the trajectory, maximum height, range and time of flight of a projectile compared with the ideal case.
Distinguish between instantaneous speed and average speed for a body undergoing non-uniform motion.
Explain why terminal speed is reached and state the condition on forces when it is achieved.
examStyle: A ball is launched horizontally from a cliff 80 m high with speed 15 m/s. Calculate (i) the time to reach the ground, (ii) the horizontal range, and (iii) the speed of impact. [6 marks]
A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 30 m/s in 8 s. Determine (i) the acceleration and (ii) the distance covered. [4 marks]
Sketch velocity-time graphs for a parachutist from jump to landing, clearly labelling terminal velocity and the moment the parachute opens. [4 marks]
A stone is thrown at 20 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. Calculate the maximum height reached and the total time of flight. [6 marks]

subtopics.title: Forces and momentum
subtopics.syllabusContent: Newton's three laws of motion. Free-body diagrams. Contact forces (normal, friction, tension, Hooke's law, viscous drag, buoyancy) and field forces (gravitational, electric, magnetic). Linear momentum, impulse, conservation of momentum, elastic and inelastic collisions, explosions. Circular motion: centripetal acceleration and force, angular velocity.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Free-body diagrams for 1D and 2D situations only. Newton's first law for translational equilibrium. Newton's third law force-pair identification. Two-dimensional collisions required for HL. Uniform and non-uniform circular motion in horizontal and vertical planes. Analysis at points other than top/bottom in vertical circular motion not required. Banked surfaces not treated quantitatively.
coreConcepts: Newton's first law: a body remains in its state of rest or uniform motion unless acted on by a resultant external force — this defines inertia.
Newton's second law: F = ma for constant mass, or F = Δp/Δt for variable mass situations; both formulations must be understood.
Newton's third law: forces always occur in equal-magnitude, opposite-direction pairs acting on different bodies — never on the same body.
Free-body diagrams must show only forces acting on the chosen system, clearly labelled with type and direction.
Linear momentum p = mv is conserved in a closed system; impulse J = FΔt equals the change in momentum.
Elastic collisions conserve both kinetic energy and momentum; inelastic collisions conserve only momentum; in explosions, momentum is also conserved.
For circular motion, centripetal acceleration a = v²/r = ω²r is always directed towards the centre; centripetal force is the resultant of real forces providing this acceleration.
Angular velocity ω relates to linear speed by v = ωr; period T = 2π/ω.
Static friction force Ff ≤ μsFN; kinetic friction Ff = μdFN; viscous drag Fd = 6πηrv; buoyancy Fb = ρVg; elastic restoring force FH = –kx.
Centripetal force is not a new or separate force — it is the label for the net inward force produced by real identified forces.
commonMisconceptions: Adding a 'centrifugal force' to a free-body diagram — this is a fictitious force; only real forces appear on free-body diagrams.
Thinking Newton's third law force pairs cancel each other — they act on different bodies and so never cancel.
Confusing weight (gravitational force on an object) with normal force — the normal force adjusts to maintain equilibrium but is not always equal to weight.
Believing momentum is conserved only in elastic collisions — momentum is conserved in all collisions; kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic ones.
Treating impulse and momentum as the same quantity — impulse (FΔt) causes the change in momentum, they have the same units but different physical meanings.
Assuming friction always opposes motion — static friction opposes the tendency of motion and can point in any direction.
Thinking a body in circular motion at constant speed has zero acceleration — it has centripetal acceleration directed inward.

conceptual: Draw a fully labelled free-body diagram for a block sliding down a rough inclined plane.
Explain, with reference to Newton's third law, why a rocket can accelerate in a vacuum.
Distinguish between elastic and inelastic collisions in terms of energy and momentum conservation.
Explain why a car rounding a level curve requires a frictional force and identify the direction of that force.
Describe what happens to the speed and kinetic energy of a satellite in a circular orbit if a small drag force acts on it.
examStyle: Two trolleys (2 kg and 3 kg) moving towards each other at 4 m/s and 2 m/s respectively collide and stick together. Calculate the velocity after collision and state whether kinetic energy is conserved. [6 marks]

A 0.5 kg ball is attached to a string and swings in a horizontal circle of radius 0.8 m with period 1.2 s. Calculate (i) the angular velocity, (ii) the centripetal acceleration, and (iii) the tension in the string. [6 marks]
A spring (k = 400 N/m) is compressed by 0.05 m. Calculate the elastic restoring force and the elastic potential energy stored. [4 marks]
Using Newton's second law in the form F = Δp/Δt, explain why crumple zones in cars reduce injury in collisions. [3 marks]

subtopics.title: Work, energy and power
subtopics.syllabusContent: Conservation of energy. Work done by a constant force W = Fs cosθ. Kinetic energy, gravitational potential energy, elastic potential energy. Work-energy theorem. Power P = ΔW/Δt = Fv. Efficiency. Sankey diagrams. Energy density of fuels.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Change in total mechanical energy relates to work done by non-conservative forces. The equation ΔEp = mgΔh applies only near Earth's surface. Energy transformations in mechanical systems should be discussed using Sankey diagrams.
coreConcepts: Work done by a force W = Fs cosθ depends on the component of force along the displacement; only that component does work.
The work-energy theorem: the net work done on a system equals its change in kinetic energy.

Conservation of mechanical energy applies in the absence of non-conservative forces (friction, air resistance); otherwise, work done by non-conservative forces equals the change in total mechanical energy.
Kinetic energy Ek = ½mv² = p²/2m; gravitational potential energy ΔEp = mgΔh (near Earth's surface); elastic potential energy EH = ½k(Δx)².
Power is the rate of energy transfer or work done: P = ΔW/Δt = Fv for constant force.
Efficiency η = useful output energy / total input energy = Poutput / Pinput; always less than 1 in real systems.
Sankey diagrams represent energy transfers with arrow widths proportional to energy magnitude, clearly showing useful output and wasted energy.
Energy density is the energy released per unit mass (or volume) of a fuel, important for comparing energy sources.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking that a force always does work — work requires displacement with a component parallel to the force; perpendicular forces do zero work.
Confusing power with energy — power is the rate of energy transfer, not the total energy transferred.
Assuming mechanical energy is always conserved — it is only conserved in the absence of friction and other dissipative forces.
Using ΔEp = mgΔh at large distances from Earth — this formula is only valid near the surface where g is approximately constant.
Treating efficiency as a percentage without understanding the physical meaning — it quantifies what fraction of input energy is usefully transferred.
Ignoring the angle θ in W = Fs cosθ — when a force is applied at an angle, only the component along the displacement does work.

conceptual: Explain why no work is done by the normal force on a body moving along a horizontal surface.
Describe using a Sankey diagram the energy transformations in a petrol engine, clearly showing useful output and wasted energy.
Explain why the efficiency of any real heat engine must be less than 100%.
Compare the energy density of hydrogen with that of diesel and discuss implications for transport.
examStyle: A 60 kg skier descends a 30° slope of length 200 m from rest. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.1. Calculate (i) the work done by gravity, (ii) the work done by friction, and (iii) the speed at the bottom. [8 marks]
A pump raises 500 kg of water per minute through a height of 10 m. Calculate the minimum power required. [4 marks]
A spring (k = 200 N/m) is compressed by 0.1 m and releases a 0.5 kg block horizontally. Determine the speed of the block when it leaves the spring. [4 marks]
An electric motor has an input power of 2000 W and an efficiency of 75%. Calculate the useful power output and the rate of energy dissipated as heat. [4 marks]

subtopics.title: Rigid body mechanics
subtopics.syllabusContent: Torque τ = Fr sinθ. Rotational equilibrium. Angular displacement, velocity and acceleration. Equations of uniform angular acceleration. Moment of inertia I = Σmr². Newton's second law for rotation τ = Iα. Angular momentum L = Iω. Conservation of angular momentum. Angular impulse ΔL = τΔt. Rotational kinetic energy Ek = ½Iω².
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Vector nature of torque and angular momentum not required; sense (clockwise/counterclockwise) must be addressed. Centre of mass calculation not required — understanding of concept sufficient. Moment of inertia equations provided when needed. Rolling without slipping is the only case of simultaneous rotation and translation required. Angular speed used rather than vector angular velocity.
coreConcepts: Torque τ = Fr sinθ is the rotational analogue of force; it measures the turning effect of a force about an axis.
Rotational equilibrium requires both the sum of forces and the sum of torques about any point to be zero.
The rotational kinematic equations are direct analogues of linear kinematic equations with θ↔s, ω↔v, α↔a.
Moment of inertia I = Σmr² represents the resistance to rotational acceleration; it depends on both mass and its distribution relative to the axis.
Newton's second law for rotation: τ = Iα; the net torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration.
Angular momentum L = Iω is conserved when no net external torque acts — analogous to linear momentum conservation.
Angular impulse τΔt = ΔL = Δ(Iω); a net torque changes angular momentum.
Rotational kinetic energy Ek = ½Iω² = L²/2I; for rolling without slipping, total KE = ½mv² + ½Iω².
Conservation of angular momentum explains phenomena such as a spinning skater pulling in arms to spin faster.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming all forces acting on a body create torque about the same axis — torque depends on the chosen axis and on the perpendicular distance.
Confusing moment of inertia with mass — I depends on how mass is distributed; a hollow cylinder has greater I than a solid cylinder of the same mass.
Applying linear conservation of momentum when angular quantities are involved — angular and linear momentum are separately conserved.
Thinking that a larger torque always means a larger angular acceleration — α = τ/I, so a large I can result in small α even with large τ.
Neglecting to specify the axis when calculating torques — the same force can have different torques about different axes.
Confusing angular speed (scalar) with angular velocity (vector) — at this level, angular speed and its sign (CW/CCW) are sufficient.

conceptual: Explain why a tightrope walker carries a long pole and why it is held horizontally.
A figure skater pulls her arms inward while spinning. Explain what happens to her angular speed and why kinetic energy changes.
Compare the moment of inertia of a solid sphere and a hollow sphere of the same mass and radius, and explain which rolls faster down an incline.
State two conditions required for a rigid body to be in static equilibrium and give a physical example of each.
examStyle: A uniform rod of mass 2 kg and length 1.2 m is pivoted at one end and held horizontal. Calculate (i) the torque of gravity about the pivot, and (ii) the vertical force needed at the free end to maintain equilibrium. [5 marks]

A flywheel (I = 0.8 kg m²) is accelerated from rest by a net torque of 4 N m. Calculate (i) the angular acceleration, (ii) the angular speed after 5 s, and (iii) the rotational kinetic energy at this point. [6 marks]

A skater (I = 4.0 kg m²) spins at 2 rad/s. She extends her arms, increasing I to 6.0 kg m². Calculate her new angular speed and the change in rotational kinetic energy. Explain why energy changes. [6 marks]
A solid cylinder (mass 3 kg, radius 0.2 m) rolls without slipping down a 5 m ramp inclined at 30°. Using energy conservation, calculate the speed at the bottom. (I_cylinder = ½MR²) [7 marks]

subtopics.title: Galilean and special relativity
subtopics.syllabusContent: Reference frames. Galilean relativity: x' = x − vt, t' = t, velocity addition u' = u − v. Postulates of special relativity. Lorentz transformations. Relativistic velocity addition. Space-time interval (invariant). Proper time and proper length. Time dilation Δt = γΔt₀. Length contraction L = L₀/γ. Relativity of simultaneity. Space-time diagrams. Muon decay as experimental evidence.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Derivation of Lorentz equations and relativistic velocity addition not required. Time axis labelled ct on space-time diagrams. World lines limited to constant velocity. Time dilation, length contraction and simultaneity can be visualized on space-time diagrams. Scales on axes of two reference frames are different, defined by lines of constant space-time interval.
coreConcepts: An inertial reference frame is one that is non-accelerating; Newton's laws hold in all inertial frames (Galilean relativity).
Galilean transformations (x' = x − vt, t' = t) assume absolute time and break down at speeds approaching c.
The two postulates of special relativity: (1) the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames; (2) the speed of light c is the same in all inertial frames.
The Lorentz factor γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²) ≥ 1 and approaches infinity as v → c, making v = c unachievable for massive objects.
Proper time Δt₀ is the time interval measured in the frame where events occur at the same location; time dilation gives Δt = γΔt₀ ≥ Δt₀.
Proper length L₀ is measured in the rest frame of the object; length contraction gives L = L₀/γ ≤ L₀ along the direction of motion only.
The space-time interval Δs² = (cΔt)² − (Δx)² is invariant — all observers agree on its value regardless of reference frame.
Simultaneity is relative: events that are simultaneous in one frame are not simultaneous in another frame moving relative to it.
Space-time (Minkowski) diagrams show world lines as paths in ct vs. x space; the angle between a world line and the ct axis is related to speed by tan θ = v/c.
Muon decay experiments confirm time dilation: muons created in the upper atmosphere survive to reach Earth's surface because their lifetime is dilated in Earth's frame.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking time dilation means clocks slow down in some absolute sense — it is a relative effect; each observer's own clock always runs normally for them.
Applying Galilean velocity addition at relativistic speeds — the relativistic formula u' = (u − v)/(1 − uv/c²) must be used.
Believing length contraction applies in all directions — it applies only along the direction of relative motion.
Confusing proper time with the longer time — proper time is the shorter time interval (γ ≥ 1, so Δt ≥ Δt₀).
Thinking the space-time interval is the same as physical distance — it is a four-dimensional invariant combining both time and space.
Assuming the speed of light can be exceeded by combining velocities classically — relativistic velocity addition ensures the resultant is always less than c.
Misreading space-time diagrams by treating the x' and ct' axes as having the same scale as x and ct — the scales differ and are defined by the invariant interval.

conceptual: State the two postulates of special relativity and explain how they conflict with Galilean relativity.
Explain why the muon decay experiment provides evidence for both time dilation and length contraction, depending on the reference frame chosen.
Describe how a space-time diagram can be used to illustrate the relativity of simultaneity.
Explain why no massive object can reach the speed of light, using the concept of the Lorentz factor.
examStyle: A spaceship travels at 0.8c relative to Earth. A clock on board measures a journey time of 5.0 years. Calculate (i) the Lorentz factor γ, (ii) the time measured on Earth, and (iii) the distance travelled according to observers on Earth. [6 marks]

Two events occur at the same location in frame S, separated by 3.0 × 10⁸ m in frame S' and a time interval of 2.0 s in S'. Calculate the space-time interval and find the proper time between the events. [6 marks]

Rocket A moves at 0.6c and fires a missile at 0.7c relative to itself in the same direction. Using the relativistic velocity addition formula, calculate the speed of the missile relative to a stationary observer. [4 marks]
Sketch a space-time diagram showing the world line of a stationary observer and a second observer moving at 0.5c. Mark a pair of events that are simultaneous in one frame but not the other. [5 marks]

topics.title: The particulate nature of matter
topics.syllabusDescription: Thermal energy transfers, greenhouse effect, gas laws, thermodynamics, and current and circuits. Links microscopic particle behaviour to macroscopic observations and explores energy transfer at molecular and macroscopic scales.

subtopics.title: Thermal energy transfers
subtopics.syllabusContent: Molecular theory of solids, liquids and gases. Density. Temperature scales (Kelvin and Celsius). Internal energy. Specific heat capacity and specific latent heat. Conduction, convection and thermal radiation. Stefan-Boltzmann law. Wien's displacement law. Luminosity and apparent brightness.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Elementary molecular model differences between states required. Kelvin-Celsius conversion required. Luminosity can be expressed in watts or in solar luminosities L⊙. The concept of apparent brightness b = L/(4πd²) required.
coreConcepts: Temperature is a measure of the average random translational kinetic energy of particles: Ek = (3/2)kBT.
Internal energy is the sum of random kinetic energy and intermolecular potential energy of all particles in a substance.
Specific heat capacity c relates heat transfer to temperature change: Q = mcΔT; specific latent heat L relates heat transfer to phase change at constant temperature: Q = mL.
Thermal conduction rate: ΔQ/Δt = kA(ΔT/Δx); depends on material conductivity, cross-sectional area, and temperature gradient.
The Stefan-Boltzmann law for a perfect black body: L = σAT⁴ gives the total power radiated.
Wien's displacement law λmaxT = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K connects peak emission wavelength to temperature.
Apparent brightness b = L/(4πd²) follows an inverse square law — a star twice as far appears four times dimmer.
Phase changes occur at constant temperature because energy input (latent heat) changes potential energy, not kinetic energy.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing heat and temperature — heat is energy in transit; temperature measures average kinetic energy per particle.
Thinking that boiling requires a temperature above 100°C — boiling point depends on pressure; at reduced pressure it occurs below 100°C.
Assuming thermal radiation requires a medium — unlike conduction and convection, radiation can transfer energy through a vacuum.
Believing all objects emit radiation only if they are glowing — all objects above 0 K emit radiation; most emit in the infrared, not visible spectrum.
Confusing luminosity and apparent brightness — luminosity is intrinsic total power; apparent brightness also depends on distance.
Thinking specific latent heat changes during a phase transition — it is approximately constant for a given material at fixed pressure.

conceptual: Explain in terms of molecular behaviour why evaporation causes cooling.
Describe, using molecular theory, why thermal conductivity differs between metals and non-metals.
Explain how Wien's displacement law allows astronomers to determine the surface temperature of a star.
Distinguish between luminosity and apparent brightness and explain the inverse square relationship.
examStyle: A 2 kg block of iron (c = 450 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) is heated from 20°C to 350°C. Calculate the thermal energy required. [3 marks]
A star has surface temperature 6000 K and radius 8 × 10⁸ m. Calculate (i) the peak wavelength of emission, and (ii) the luminosity of the star. [5 marks]
The rate of thermal energy conduction through a glass window (k = 1.0 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, area 2 m², thickness 4 mm) with a temperature difference of 15°C is to be calculated. [4 marks]
200 g of ice at 0°C is added to 500 g of water at 80°C. Determine whether all ice melts and find the final temperature. (Lf = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹, c_water = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) [7 marks]

subtopics.title: Greenhouse effect
subtopics.syllabusContent: Conservation of energy. Emissivity. Albedo. Solar constant S. Greenhouse gases (CH₄, H₂O, CO₂, N₂O) and molecular energy levels. Resonance model and molecular energy levels to explain greenhouse effect. Enhanced greenhouse effect.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Problems include estimation of equilibrium temperature using energy balance (albedo, emissivity, solar constant). Energy balance includes surface-atmosphere exchange. Burning fossil fuels is primary cause of enhanced greenhouse effect.
coreConcepts: Emissivity ε = (power radiated per unit area) / σT⁴; a perfect black body has ε = 1; real surfaces have 0 < ε < 1.
Albedo = total scattered power / total incident power; Earth's albedo varies with cloud cover, ice cover, and latitude.
The solar constant S ≈ 1361 W m⁻² is the power per unit area received by Earth from the Sun at the mean Earth-Sun distance.
Energy balance: incoming intensity S/4 (averaged over Earth's spherical surface) equals outgoing radiated power for equilibrium temperature.
Greenhouse gases (CH₄, H₂O, CO₂, N₂O) absorb infrared radiation through molecular vibrational energy transitions and re-emit in all directions, trapping energy.
The enhanced greenhouse effect refers to the additional warming caused by human-produced increases in greenhouse gas concentrations.
Equilibrium temperature: (1 − albedo) × S/4 = εσT⁴; solving gives the planet's effective surface temperature.
Without any greenhouse effect, Earth's surface temperature would be approximately −18°C; actual average is about +15°C.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing the greenhouse effect with ozone depletion — they are separate atmospheric phenomena with different mechanisms and gases.
Thinking albedo is fixed — it changes seasonally, with land use change, snow/ice melt, and cloud cover.
Assuming all electromagnetic radiation is trapped by the greenhouse effect — only infrared (thermal) radiation is primarily absorbed by greenhouse gases.
Believing the greenhouse effect is entirely harmful — without the natural greenhouse effect, Earth would be too cold to support life.
Thinking CO₂ is the most abundant greenhouse gas — water vapour H₂O is the most abundant, but CO₂ is the most significant anthropogenic contributor.
Confusing emissivity with reflectivity — emissivity relates to radiation emitted; albedo/reflectivity relates to radiation reflected.

conceptual: Explain, using molecular energy levels, how CO₂ absorbs infrared radiation and contributes to the greenhouse effect.
Describe how the enhanced greenhouse effect differs from the natural greenhouse effect.
Explain why Earth's albedo varies with latitude and season.
examStyle: A planet has albedo 0.30, emissivity 1.0, and receives a mean intensity of 340 W m⁻². Calculate its equilibrium temperature. [4 marks]
Explain why melting Arctic sea ice creates a positive feedback loop that amplifies the enhanced greenhouse effect. [4 marks]
Calculate the change in equilibrium temperature if Earth's albedo decreases from 0.30 to 0.25 due to reduced ice cover, assuming all other quantities remain constant. [5 marks]

subtopics.title: Gas laws
subtopics.syllabusContent: Pressure P = F/A. Amount of substance n. Ideal gas assumptions (kinetic theory). Combined gas law PV/T = constant. Ideal gas equations PV = NkBT and PV = nRT. Pressure from kinetic theory P = (1/3)ρv². Internal energy of monatomic ideal gas U = (3/2)NkBT. Conditions under which ideal gas approximates real gas.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Kinetic model assumptions required. Differences between ideal and real gases must be understood. Gas laws limited to constant volume, constant temperature, constant pressure and the ideal gas law. Qualitative explanation of macroscopic properties in terms of molecular behaviour required. P-V diagrams used for state changes.
coreConcepts: Ideal gas assumptions: point particles with no intermolecular forces, perfectly elastic collisions, random motion.
The ideal gas equation PV = nRT = NkBT unifies Boyle's law (P∝1/V at constant T), Charles's law (V∝T at constant P), and Gay-Lussac's law (P∝T at constant V).
Pressure arises from the rate of change of momentum of particles colliding with the container walls: P = (1/3)ρv².
Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas: U = (3/2)NkBT = (3/2)nRT; only kinetic energy (no potential energy between particles in ideal gas).
The Boltzmann constant kB = R/NA links macroscopic thermodynamics (R) to microscopic particle energy.
Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour at high pressure (particles no longer negligible volume) and low temperature (intermolecular attractions significant).
P-V diagrams represent isotherms (constant T) as hyperbolas for ideal gases; changes of state can be plotted and areas under curves related to work.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming ideal gas laws apply under all conditions — they break down at high pressure and low temperature where real gas behaviour dominates.
Confusing the number of molecules N with the amount of substance n — N = nNA where NA is Avogadro's number.
Thinking temperature in gas law equations can be in Celsius — all gas law calculations require absolute temperature in Kelvin.
Assuming the internal energy of an ideal gas includes potential energy — for an ideal gas, internal energy is purely kinetic.
Misinterpreting rms speed as the actual speed of any single particle — it is a statistical root-mean-square average of all particle speeds.

conceptual: Explain using kinetic theory why the pressure of a gas increases when its temperature increases at constant volume.
Describe the assumptions of the kinetic model of an ideal gas and explain which are violated at high pressure.
Explain why temperature must be measured in Kelvin when applying the ideal gas law.
examStyle: A fixed amount of ideal gas is at 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa, volume 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³, and temperature 300 K. It is heated to 450 K at constant pressure. Calculate the new volume. [4 marks]
Calculate the rms speed of nitrogen molecules (M = 0.028 kg mol⁻¹) at 27°C. [4 marks]
0.5 mol of ideal monatomic gas is at temperature 400 K. Calculate (i) the internal energy and (ii) the average kinetic energy per molecule. [4 marks]
Sketch a P-V diagram showing an isothermal compression followed by a constant-volume pressure increase to return to the original pressure. Label all states and processes. [4 marks]

subtopics.title: Thermodynamics
subtopics.syllabusContent: First law of thermodynamics Q = ΔU + W. Work done by a gas W = PΔV. Change in internal energy of monatomic ideal gas. Entropy S = kB ln Ω. Second law of thermodynamics. Isothermal, isobaric, isovolumetric and adiabatic processes. PV^(5/3) = constant for monatomic ideal gas adiabatic process. Cyclic processes and heat engines. Carnot efficiency ηCarnot = 1 − Tc/Th.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Closed system: no mass transfer; isolated system: no mass or energy transfer. Clausius sign convention: Q is thermal energy supplied to the system; W is work done by the system. Second law in Clausius form, Kelvin form, and entropy form. Quantitative problems limited to monatomic ideal gases. Microstates described through simple combinatorial models.
coreConcepts: First law: Q = ΔU + W — the heat supplied to a system increases its internal energy and/or enables it to do work on the surroundings.
Work done by a gas W = PΔV; work done on a gas is taken as negative in the Clausius convention.
Entropy S = kB ln Ω quantifies microscopic disorder; macroscopically ΔS = ΔQ/T for reversible processes.
Second law: in an isolated system, entropy never decreases; real processes are irreversible and increase total entropy.
Processes: isothermal (T constant, ΔU = 0), isobaric (P constant, W = PΔV), isovolumetric (V constant, W = 0), adiabatic (Q = 0, PV^γ = constant).
The Carnot cycle is the idealized reversible cycle operating between two temperatures; its efficiency ηCarnot = 1 − Tc/Th is the maximum achievable.
No real engine can be 100% efficient — some energy must always be transferred to the cold reservoir (second law).
A non-isolated system's entropy can decrease locally, but this is always offset by equal or greater increase in the surroundings.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing the first law with energy conservation in general — it specifically relates heat, work and internal energy in thermodynamic systems.
Thinking that adiabatic means isothermal — in an adiabatic process Q = 0 but temperature can still change (ΔU = −W).
Assuming the Carnot efficiency is achievable in practice — it requires perfect reversibility, which no real engine achieves.
Believing entropy is a measure of disorder in a vague qualitative sense only — it has a precise mathematical definition in terms of microstates.
Confusing the sign of work: work done by the gas is positive (expansion), work done on the gas is negative under Clausius convention.
Assuming entropy can decrease in isolated systems — the second law prohibits this; only in non-isolated systems can local entropy decrease.

Thinking all reversible engines have the same efficiency regardless of operating temperatures — only the Carnot cycle achieves maximum efficiency; real reversible cycles operating between the same temperatures also achieve Carnot efficiency.

conceptual: State the second law of thermodynamics in (i) Clausius form, (ii) Kelvin form, and (iii) entropy form.
Explain why the efficiency of any real heat engine is always less than the Carnot efficiency.
Describe what happens to the internal energy, work done, and heat exchange in an adiabatic compression of a monatomic ideal gas.
Using the concept of microstates, explain why a gas spreads to fill its container rather than spontaneously contracting.
examStyle: A monatomic ideal gas (1 mol) is heated at constant volume from 300 K to 500 K. Calculate (i) the change in internal energy, (ii) the work done, and (iii) the heat supplied. [6 marks]

A Carnot engine operates between temperatures 800 K and 300 K. Calculate its efficiency. If the engine absorbs 5000 J per cycle from the hot reservoir, find the work output and heat rejected. [6 marks]

An ideal gas undergoes the cycle: isothermal expansion A→B, isovolumetric cooling B→C, isobaric compression C→A. Sketch the cycle on a P-V diagram and determine whether the net work done by the gas is positive or negative. [6 marks]
State and explain one way in which a power station turbine could be made to operate closer to Carnot efficiency, and discuss practical limitations. [4 marks]

subtopics.title: Current and circuits
subtopics.syllabusContent: EMF and internal resistance. Circuit diagrams. Direct current I = Δq/Δt. Potential difference V = W/q. Resistance R = V/I. Resistivity ρ = RA/L. Ohm's law. Ohmic and non-ohmic conductors. Power P = IV = I²R = V²/R. Series and parallel combinations. Internal resistance ε = I(R + r). Variable resistors (thermistor, LDR, potentiometer).
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Advantages and disadvantages of different energy sources required. AC circuits not required. Ideal ammeters and voltmeters assumed unless stated otherwise. Metal conductor at constant temperature is ohmic. Variable resistors limited to thermistors, LDRs and potentiometers.
coreConcepts: EMF ε is the energy supplied per unit charge by the source; terminal voltage is less than EMF when current flows due to internal resistance: ε = I(R + r).
Potential difference V = W/q is the work done per unit charge moved between two points; it drives current through resistance.
Ohm's law: V = IR applies to ohmic conductors at constant temperature; non-ohmic devices (diodes, filament bulbs, thermistors) have non-linear V-I characteristics.
Resistivity ρ = RA/L is an intrinsic material property; resistance R depends also on geometry (length and cross-sectional area).
Series circuits: same current through all components; voltages add; resistances add: Rs = R1 + R2 + ...
Parallel circuits: same voltage across all branches; currents add; 1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ...
Power dissipated: P = IV = I²R = V²/R; heating effect of a resistor converts electrical energy to thermal energy.
Thermistors have resistance that decreases with temperature (NTC type); LDRs have resistance that decreases with light intensity; both are non-ohmic.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing EMF with potential difference — EMF is the energy per charge supplied by the source; PD is the energy per charge transferred between two points in the circuit.
Thinking current is 'used up' as it flows around a circuit — current (charge flow rate) is the same everywhere in a series circuit.
Assuming adding resistors in parallel always increases resistance — it decreases the total resistance; total parallel resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistance.
Believing Ohm's law applies to all materials — it applies only to ohmic conductors under constant conditions; most real devices are non-ohmic.
Confusing internal resistance with external resistance — internal resistance causes a drop in terminal voltage when current flows.
Thinking power dissipation depends only on resistance — it depends on both resistance and current (or voltage); P = I²R shows it depends on current squared.

conceptual: Explain, using a particle model, why the resistance of a metal conductor increases with temperature.
Describe the V-I characteristics of a filament bulb and explain why it is non-ohmic.
Explain the difference between the EMF and terminal voltage of a battery when it is supplying current.
Describe how a potential divider circuit using an LDR could be used as a light sensor to turn on a lamp.
examStyle: A battery of EMF 12 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω drives a current through an external resistor of 3.5 Ω. Calculate (i) the current, (ii) the terminal voltage, and (iii) the power dissipated in the internal resistance. [6 marks]

Three resistors (6 Ω, 12 Ω, 4 Ω) are connected: the 6 Ω and 12 Ω are in parallel, and this combination is in series with the 4 Ω. Calculate the total resistance and the current from a 24 V supply. [5 marks]
A copper wire (ρ = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m, length 5.0 m, diameter 0.5 mm) carries a current of 2 A. Calculate the resistance and the power dissipated. [5 marks]
Sketch and explain the V-I characteristics of (i) a resistor at constant temperature and (ii) a semiconductor diode. [4 marks]

topics.title: Wave behaviour
topics.syllabusDescription: Simple harmonic motion, wave model, wave phenomena (reflection, refraction, diffraction, interference), standing waves, resonance and the Doppler effect. Links oscillation theory to wave behaviour across mechanical and electromagnetic contexts.

subtopics.title: Simple harmonic motion
subtopics.syllabusContent: Conditions for SHM. Defining equation a = −ω²x. Period, frequency, angular frequency, amplitude. Period of mass-spring system T = 2π√(m/k). Period of simple pendulum T = 2π√(l/g). Phase angle. Equations x = x₀ sin(ωt + φ), v = ωx₀ cos(ωt + φ). Energy: ET = ½mω²x₀², Ep = ½mω²x².
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Significance of the minus sign in a = −ω²x must be understood. Qualitative energy description at SL; quantitative at HL. Radians used for phase angle. Simple pendulum approximation valid for small angles only.
coreConcepts: SHM requires a restoring force proportional to and directed opposite to displacement from equilibrium: F = −kx, leading to a = −ω²x.
The minus sign in a = −ω²x is fundamental — it ensures acceleration always points back towards equilibrium, creating oscillation.
Angular frequency ω = 2πf = 2π/T; for a mass-spring system ω = √(k/m); for a simple pendulum ω = √(g/l).
Phase angle φ determines the initial conditions; x = x₀ sin(ωt + φ) and v = ωx₀ cos(ωt + φ).
Total mechanical energy ET = ½mω²x₀² is constant; it is shared between Ek = ½mω²(x₀² − x²) and Ep = ½mω²x².
Maximum speed occurs at x = 0 (equilibrium): vmax = ωx₀; maximum acceleration occurs at x = ±x₀: amax = ω²x₀.
The simple pendulum approximation (T = 2π√(l/g)) holds only for small amplitudes (θ < ~10°).
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a = −ω²x implies acceleration is always negative — it means acceleration is in the opposite direction to displacement.
Confusing angular frequency ω with ordinary frequency f — they are related by ω = 2πf and have different units (rad s⁻¹ vs Hz).
Assuming maximum velocity occurs at maximum displacement — it occurs at the equilibrium position where all energy is kinetic.
Believing the period of a simple pendulum depends on the mass of the bob — it depends only on length and g.
Forgetting that the pendulum formula is only valid for small angles — large-amplitude pendulums have longer periods than predicted by T = 2π√(l/g).
Confusing total energy with maximum kinetic energy — they are equal only when the oscillator passes through equilibrium.

conceptual: Explain why the motion of a mass on a spring is SHM, stating the condition on the restoring force.
Describe the energy transformations during one complete oscillation of a simple pendulum, starting from maximum displacement.
Explain the physical significance of the minus sign in the defining equation a = −ω²x.
Sketch displacement-time and velocity-time graphs for a particle undergoing SHM, starting from equilibrium.
examStyle: A mass of 0.4 kg on a spring (k = 160 N/m) is displaced 0.05 m from equilibrium. Calculate (i) the angular frequency, (ii) the period, (iii) the maximum speed, and (iv) the total energy. [8 marks]
A pendulum of length 0.6 m is displaced 0.08 m from equilibrium. Calculate (i) the period, (ii) the maximum acceleration, and (iii) the speed when displacement is 0.04 m. [6 marks]
The displacement of a particle is given by x = 0.02 sin(10t + π/3) m. Determine (i) the amplitude, (ii) the angular frequency, (iii) the phase angle, and (iv) the velocity at t = 0. [6 marks]
Sketch a graph of kinetic energy and potential energy against displacement for a SHM oscillator. Describe how the total energy varies. [4 marks]

subtopics.title: Wave model
subtopics.syllabusContent: Transverse and longitudinal waves. Wavelength, frequency, period, wave speed: v = fλ. Sound waves. Electromagnetic waves. Differences between mechanical and electromagnetic waves.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Problems involve describing particle motion in both transverse and longitudinal waves. Travelling waves transfer energy without net displacement of medium. Approximate wavelength orders of magnitude for EM spectrum required.
coreConcepts: In transverse waves, particle oscillation is perpendicular to wave propagation direction; in longitudinal waves, oscillation is parallel.
Wave speed v = fλ = λ/T; all three quantities are linked and changing one (e.g., medium change) affects the others.
Mechanical waves require a medium for propagation (sound, water waves); electromagnetic waves do not and travel at c in a vacuum.
All electromagnetic waves travel at c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum and form a continuous spectrum from radio waves to gamma rays.
Sound waves are longitudinal pressure waves; compressions and rarefactions describe regions of high and low pressure.
Travelling waves transfer energy in the direction of propagation without permanently displacing the medium.
The EM spectrum (in order of increasing frequency): radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma ray.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking matter moves in the direction of wave propagation for all waves — only for longitudinal waves; transverse waves have perpendicular particle motion.
Assuming the wave speed changes with frequency or amplitude — wave speed depends on the medium, not on frequency or amplitude.
Believing sound can travel through a vacuum — sound is a mechanical wave requiring a physical medium.
Confusing wavelength with amplitude — wavelength is the spatial period of the wave; amplitude is the maximum displacement of particles.
Thinking all EM waves have the same energy — energy of a photon E = hf, so higher frequency EM waves (gamma) carry more energy than lower frequency (radio) waves.

conceptual: Describe the motion of air particles as a sound wave passes through them, distinguishing compressions and rarefactions.
Explain two differences between electromagnetic waves and mechanical waves.
A wave travels from air into glass. Explain what happens to the wavelength, frequency and wave speed.
examStyle: A sound wave has frequency 440 Hz and travels at 340 m/s in air. Calculate the wavelength. [2 marks]
An EM wave has wavelength 500 nm. Calculate its frequency and state which part of the EM spectrum it belongs to. [3 marks]
Sketch displacement-position graphs for (i) a transverse wave and (ii) a longitudinal wave, clearly indicating particle displacement directions. [4 marks]

subtopics.title: Wave phenomena
subtopics.syllabusContent: Wavefronts and rays. Reflection, refraction, transmission. Diffraction. Snell's law, critical angle, total internal reflection. Superposition. Coherent sources. Conditions for constructive and destructive interference. Young's double-slit: s = λD/d. Single-slit diffraction: θ = λ/b. Single-slit pattern modulates double-slit pattern. Diffraction grating: nλ = d sinθ.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Sketching and interpreting wavefronts and rays limited to incident, reflected and transmitted waves. Interference and diffraction patterns at normal incidence only. Effect of slit width on intensity qualitatively considered. Single-slit limited to monochromatic light and rectangular slits. Multiple slit and diffraction grating patterns for white light and monochromatic light.
coreConcepts: Snell's law: n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂; the refractive index n = c/v relates to how much light slows in the medium.
Total internal reflection occurs when light travels from a denser to less dense medium and the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle: sinθc = n₂/n₁.
Constructive interference: path difference = nλ; destructive interference: path difference = (n + ½)λ.
Young's double-slit fringe spacing: s = λD/d; increasing slit separation d decreases fringe spacing; increasing wavelength increases it.
Single-slit diffraction: first minimum at θ = λ/b; narrower slits produce wider diffraction patterns.
The double-slit interference pattern is modulated (multiplied) by the single-slit diffraction envelope — some bright fringes may be missing.
Diffraction grating: nλ = d sinθ where d is grating spacing; gratings produce sharper, brighter maxima than double slits.
Coherent sources have a constant phase relationship — essential for a stable interference pattern.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking diffraction only occurs with waves — it is a universal wave phenomenon; all waves including sound and electrons diffract.
Confusing refraction with reflection — refraction is the change in direction due to change in speed when entering a new medium; reflection is the return of the wave.
Assuming more slits give a brighter but broader pattern — more slits produce sharper (narrower) and brighter principal maxima.
Believing interference requires two separate sources — coherent light from the same source split by a double slit produces interference.
Confusing constructive and destructive interference conditions — constructive: path difference = nλ; destructive: path difference = (n + ½)λ.
Thinking the critical angle is the angle of refraction, not incidence — it is the angle of incidence beyond which TIR occurs.

conceptual: Explain what is meant by coherent sources and why coherence is necessary for a stable interference pattern.
Describe how the fringe pattern from a Young's double-slit experiment changes if (i) the slit separation is halved, (ii) blue light replaces red light.
Explain how a diffraction grating can be used to measure the wavelength of light, including the relevant equation.
Describe the conditions under which total internal reflection occurs and give one practical application.
examStyle: Monochromatic light (λ = 620 nm) passes through a double slit (d = 0.4 mm) and produces fringes on a screen 1.5 m away. Calculate the fringe spacing. [3 marks]
Light travels from glass (n = 1.5) into air. Calculate the critical angle and describe what happens when the angle of incidence exceeds this value. [4 marks]
A diffraction grating has 600 lines per mm. Light of wavelength 550 nm is incident normally. Calculate the angle of the second-order maximum. [4 marks]
Sketch the intensity pattern for single-slit diffraction and explain how the pattern would change if the slit width is halved. [4 marks]

subtopics.title: Standing waves and resonance
subtopics.syllabusContent: Formation of standing waves by superposition of two identical waves travelling in opposite directions. Nodes, antinodes, amplitude, phase. Standing waves in strings and pipes. Resonance: natural frequency, driving frequency, damping effects. Light, critical and heavy damping.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Standing waves from superposition of more than two waves not considered. Pipes referred to as open or closed. End corrections not required. Boundary conditions for strings and pipes specified. Lowest frequency mode = first harmonic (not fundamental). Qualitative analysis only for damping effect on resonance frequency. Useful and destructive resonance effects required.
coreConcepts: Standing waves form when two identical waves travel in opposite directions and superpose; nodes have zero displacement, antinodes have maximum displacement.
For a string fixed at both ends or pipe open at both ends: L = nλ/2, f = nv/2L (harmonics: n = 1, 2, 3, ...).
For a pipe closed at one end: L = nλ/4 with n odd only; f = nv/4L (only odd harmonics: n = 1, 3, 5, ...).
Resonance occurs when a driving frequency matches the natural frequency, leading to maximum amplitude of oscillation.
Damping reduces the maximum amplitude at resonance and causes the resonant frequency to shift slightly below the natural frequency.
Light damping: oscillations persist but decrease slowly; critical damping: fastest return to equilibrium without oscillating; heavy damping: slow return without oscillating.
At nodes, particles are always at rest and have a phase difference of 0 with each other; at antinodes, particles oscillate with maximum amplitude.
Adjacent nodes (or antinodes) are separated by λ/2; the wavelength of the standing wave equals twice the distance between adjacent nodes.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking standing waves transfer energy like travelling waves — in an ideal standing wave, there is no net energy transfer along the medium.
Confusing nodes and antinodes — nodes are points of zero displacement; antinodes are points of maximum displacement.
Assuming all harmonics exist in a closed pipe — only odd harmonics are present in a pipe closed at one end.
Confusing resonant frequency with natural frequency — damping reduces the resonant frequency slightly below the natural frequency.
Thinking more damping always reduces the resonant frequency significantly — heavy damping eliminates resonance entirely; light damping causes only a small frequency shift.
Believing standing waves only occur in musical instruments — they occur in any system with appropriate boundary conditions (microwave ovens, laser cavities).

conceptual: Explain how a standing wave is formed and describe the difference between nodes and antinodes.
Describe the first three harmonics (standing wave patterns) for a string fixed at both ends.
Explain the difference between light, critical and heavy damping in terms of motion after the driving force is removed.
Give one useful and one potentially destructive application of resonance.
examStyle: A string of length 0.9 m is fixed at both ends and vibrates in its third harmonic. If the wave speed is 180 m/s, calculate (i) the wavelength and (ii) the frequency. [4 marks]
A closed pipe of length 0.4 m resonates in its first harmonic. Calculate the frequency, given the speed of sound is 340 m/s. State which harmonics are present for this type of pipe. [4 marks]
Sketch a resonance curve for a lightly damped oscillator. On the same axes, sketch the curve for a more heavily damped oscillator. Label natural frequency and maximum amplitude. [4 marks]

subtopics.title: Doppler effect
subtopics.syllabusContent: Doppler effect for sound and electromagnetic waves. Wavefront diagrams. Relative frequency shift for light: Δf/f ≈ Δλ/λ ≈ v/c. Spectral line shifts. Moving source: f' = fv/(v ± us). Moving observer: f' = f(v ± uo)/v.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Problems not involving both source and observer moving simultaneously. Problems can involve determining velocity of source/observer. Doppler effect applied in medical physics (ultrasound) and radar. Signs: + when source/observer approaches, − when receding (check conventions carefully).
coreConcepts: The Doppler effect: when source and observer move relative to each other, the observed frequency differs from the emitted frequency.
Approaching source/observer: observed frequency is higher (blue shift); receding: lower (red shift).
For sound, moving source: f' = fv/(v ∓ us) (− when approaching, + when receding); moving observer: f' = f(v ± uo)/v (+ approaching, − receding).
For electromagnetic waves (v << c): Δf/f ≈ Δλ/λ ≈ v/c gives the fractional shift due to relative motion.
Shifts in spectral lines allow astronomers to determine whether stars and galaxies are moving towards or away from Earth and their speed.
Medical ultrasound uses the Doppler effect to measure blood flow velocity by detecting frequency shifts in reflected sound pulses.
Radar speed measurement uses the Doppler shift of reflected radio waves to determine the speed of a moving target.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking the Doppler effect changes the speed of the wave — it changes only the observed frequency and wavelength; wave speed is unchanged.
Confusing the formulas for moving source and moving observer — the two formulas are different and must be applied correctly depending on which is moving.
Assuming the Doppler formula for sound applies directly to light — for light, the relativistic formula applies; at v << c, the approximate form Δf/f ≈ v/c is used.
Thinking redshift always means a galaxy is moving away — cosmological redshift is due to expansion of space, not purely to relative velocity.
Applying incorrect signs (+ and −) in the Doppler formulas — careful attention to whether the source/observer is approaching or receding is required.

conceptual: Explain, using a wavefront diagram, why the frequency of sound heard by an observer increases as a source approaches.
Describe how the Doppler effect is used in medical ultrasound to measure blood flow velocity.
Explain how the redshift of spectral lines from distant galaxies provides evidence for the expansion of the universe.
examStyle: A police siren emits sound at 800 Hz. The police car moves at 30 m/s towards a stationary observer. Calculate the observed frequency. (Speed of sound = 340 m/s) [3 marks]
A star emits light at 486 nm (Hβ line) but astronomers observe it at 490 nm. Calculate the speed of the star and state whether it is moving towards or away from Earth. [4 marks]

A bat emits ultrasound at 50 kHz and flies at 8 m/s towards a stationary wall. Calculate (i) the frequency reflected from the wall and (ii) the frequency heard by the bat in the reflected wave. (Speed of sound = 340 m/s) [6 marks]

topics.title: Fields
topics.syllabusDescription: Gravitational fields, electric and magnetic fields, motion in electromagnetic fields, and electromagnetic induction. Develops field theory from Newtonian gravitation through electrostatics and magnetism to Faraday's law.

subtopics.title: Gravitational fields
subtopics.syllabusContent: Kepler's three laws. Newton's law of universal gravitation F = Gm₁m₂/r². Gravitational field strength g = F/m = GM/r². Gravitational potential energy Ep = −Gm₁m₂/r. Gravitational potential Vg = −GM/r. Gravitational potential gradient g = −ΔVg/Δr. Escape speed. Orbital speed. Equipotential surfaces. Effect of atmospheric drag on orbiting bodies.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Circular orbits assumed for calculations. Spherical masses treated as point masses at centre. Resultant field limited to points along line joining two bodies. Gravitational potential defined as zero at infinity. Problems include orbital speed, energy changes between orbits, launching into orbit and escape energy.
coreConcepts: Newton's universal law: F = Gm₁m₂/r²; gravitational force is always attractive, acts along the line joining the centres of mass.
Gravitational field strength g = GM/r² is the force per unit mass at a point; near Earth's surface g ≈ 9.8 m s⁻².
Gravitational potential Vg = −GM/r is the work done per unit mass in bringing a test mass from infinity to that point; it is always negative.
Gravitational potential energy Ep = −Gm₁m₂/r; the negative sign reflects that energy must be supplied to separate masses to infinity.
Orbital speed: vorbital = √(GM/r); escape speed: vesc = √(2GM/r); note vesc = √2 × vorbital.
Kepler's first law: elliptical orbits; second law: equal areas in equal times (conservation of angular momentum); third law: T² ∝ r³.
Equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to field lines; no work is done moving along an equipotential.
A satellite in a decaying orbit due to atmospheric drag loses energy, speeds up, and descends to a lower orbit — paradoxically, drag causes the satellite to accelerate.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking gravitational potential is always positive — it is defined as zero at infinity and is negative for any finite distance from a mass.
Confusing gravitational potential energy with gravitational potential — Ep = mVg; potential energy depends on the test mass, potential does not.
Assuming a satellite in a circular orbit is weightless because gravity is absent — gravity provides the centripetal force; weightlessness is apparent and due to free fall.
Thinking escape speed means the satellite never returns — it is the minimum launch speed from rest to escape gravity; rockets can escape at lower speeds with continuous thrust.
Confusing the direction of g with the direction of increasing potential — g points towards decreasing potential (from high to low Vg is wrong; Vg is always negative, g = −ΔVg/Δr).
Believing a satellite with atmospheric drag slows down and rises — the drag causes energy loss, the orbit shrinks, and the satellite actually speeds up at lower altitude.

conceptual: Explain why the gravitational potential is always negative and why it is defined as zero at infinity.
Describe, using energy considerations, how atmospheric drag causes a satellite to speed up rather than slow down as it spirals inward.
State Kepler's three laws and explain how the third law can be derived from Newton's law of gravitation for circular orbits.
Sketch gravitational field lines and equipotential surfaces around two equal point masses and explain the relationship between them.
examStyle: A satellite of mass 500 kg orbits Earth (M = 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg, R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m) at an altitude of 400 km. Calculate (i) the orbital speed, (ii) the period, and (iii) the total mechanical energy of the satellite. [8 marks]
Calculate the escape speed from the surface of the Moon (M = 7.3 × 10²² kg, R = 1.7 × 10⁶ m) and compare with Earth's escape speed. [5 marks]
Two stars of masses 2M and 3M are separated by distance d. Determine the point along the line joining them where the net gravitational field strength is zero. [5 marks]

A spacecraft moves from orbit at r₁ = 8 × 10⁶ m to r₂ = 16 × 10⁶ m from Earth's centre. Calculate the change in gravitational potential energy and state whether energy must be supplied or released. [5 marks]

subtopics.title: Electric and magnetic fields
subtopics.syllabusContent: Coulomb's law F = kq₁q₂/r². Electric field strength E = F/q. Uniform field E = V/d. Millikan's experiment. Charge transfer methods. Electric potential Ve = kQ/r. Electric potential energy Ep = kq₁q₂/r. Potential gradient E = −ΔVe/Δr. Equipotential surfaces. Magnetic field lines and patterns for bar magnet, wire, coil, solenoid.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Electric fields include radial (point charge), inside/outside conducting sphere, between two charges, between parallel plates with edge effects. Magnetic field patterns for bar magnet, current-carrying straight wire, circular coil, solenoid required. Work in electronvolts and joules. Electric potential zero at infinity.
coreConcepts: Coulomb's law: F = kq₁q₂/r² where k = 1/(4πε₀); force is attractive for opposite charges, repulsive for like charges.
Electric field strength E = F/q is the force per unit positive charge; for a uniform field between parallel plates E = V/d.
Electric potential Ve = kQ/r; it is a scalar, defined as zero at infinity; for positive charges Ve is positive, for negative charges it is negative.
Electric potential energy Ep = kq₁q₂/r; work done moving charge q through potential difference ΔV is W = qΔV.
The electric field points from high to low potential; E = −ΔVe/Δr (field is the negative of potential gradient).
Millikan's experiment demonstrated the quantization of charge by balancing gravitational and electric forces on charged oil droplets: qE = mg.
Magnetic field lines form closed loops; they emerge from N poles and enter S poles; right-hand rule determines field direction around current-carrying conductors.
Equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to electric field lines; no work is done moving a charge along an equipotential.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking electric potential and electric field have the same direction — potential is a scalar; field is a vector pointing from high to low potential.
Assuming electric field inside a conductor is non-zero — in electrostatic equilibrium, the field inside a conductor is zero.
Confusing electric potential energy and electric potential — Ep = qVe; potential is a property of the field, potential energy also depends on the charge.
Believing magnetic field lines start and end on poles like electric field lines on charges — magnetic field lines are always closed loops; there are no magnetic monopoles.
Thinking Coulomb's law applies to extended charge distributions without modification — it applies to point charges; for spherical conductors, charge is treated as concentrated at the centre.

conceptual: Explain why the electric field inside a hollow conducting sphere is zero even when charge is distributed on its outer surface.
Describe the Millikan oil drop experiment and explain how it provides evidence for charge quantization.
Sketch the electric field lines and equipotential surfaces for (i) a single positive charge and (ii) two equal and opposite charges (an electric dipole).
Explain the analogy between gravitational and electric fields, including both similarities and one key difference.
examStyle: Two point charges +4 μC and −2 μC are separated by 0.3 m. Calculate (i) the force between them, (ii) the electric field at the midpoint, and (iii) the electric potential at the midpoint. [8 marks]

Parallel plates are 5 mm apart with a potential difference of 500 V. A proton enters midway between the plates moving parallel to them at 2 × 10⁵ m/s. Calculate the deflection of the proton as it exits the plates (length 0.1 m). [7 marks]

In Millikan's experiment, an oil drop of mass 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg is held stationary in a field of 4.0 × 10⁴ V/m. Calculate the charge on the drop and determine how many elementary charges this represents. [4 marks]
Sketch the magnetic field pattern for a current-carrying solenoid. State how the field inside compares to outside and identify where the field is most uniform. [4 marks]

subtopics.title: Motion in electromagnetic fields
subtopics.syllabusContent: Motion of charged particles in uniform electric fields. Motion in uniform magnetic fields: F = qvB sinθ. Combined perpendicular E and B fields (velocity selector). Force on current-carrying conductor F = BIL sinθ. Force per unit length between parallel wires F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πr).
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Kinetic energy constant in magnetic field. Charge-to-mass ratio determined from circular path in magnetic field. Direction of force using Fleming's left-hand rule or right-hand rule. Parallel currents in same direction attract; opposite directions repel.
coreConcepts: Force on a moving charge in a magnetic field: F = qvB sinθ, perpendicular to both velocity and field — causes circular motion without doing work.
A charged particle moving perpendicularly to a uniform magnetic field undergoes circular motion: qvB = mv²/r, so r = mv/(qB).
The charge-to-mass ratio q/m = v/(Br) can be determined by measuring the radius of circular motion in a known magnetic field.
A velocity selector uses perpendicular E and B fields such that only particles with v = E/B pass undeflected.
Force on a current-carrying conductor: F = BIL sinθ; direction given by Fleming's left-hand rule.
Force per unit length between two parallel wires: F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πr); wires with currents in the same direction attract.
In a uniform electric field, a charged particle undergoes constant acceleration (analogous to projectile motion).
The magnetic force never does work on a charged particle — it can only change direction, not speed or kinetic energy.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking the magnetic force does work on a moving charge — the magnetic force is always perpendicular to velocity; work = F·d requires a parallel component, so W = 0.
Assuming a charged particle moving parallel to B experiences a magnetic force — F = qvB sinθ = 0 when θ = 0.
Confusing the direction of force using the wrong hand rule — for positive charges (conventional current), use the left-hand rule for motor effect; electrons need the opposite.
Thinking the radius of circular motion in a magnetic field depends on speed in all cases — r = mv/(qB) shows radius increases with speed, not that it is independent.
Believing parallel wires repel each other when currents flow in the same direction — they attract; opposite current directions cause repulsion.

conceptual: Explain why a magnetic force does no work on a moving charged particle and what consequence this has for its motion.
Describe the operation of a velocity selector, including the condition for a particle to pass undeflected.
Explain how the charge-to-mass ratio of an electron can be determined from observing its circular path in a uniform magnetic field.
examStyle: An electron (m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at 3.0 × 10⁶ m/s perpendicular to a magnetic field of 0.02 T. Calculate (i) the magnetic force, (ii) the radius of circular motion, and (iii) the period of revolution. [6 marks]

Two parallel wires 0.5 m long are 4 cm apart. Wire 1 carries 3 A and wire 2 carries 5 A in the same direction. Calculate the force between them and state whether it is attractive or repulsive. [4 marks]
A proton enters a velocity selector with E = 5000 V/m and B = 0.01 T. Calculate the speed of protons that pass through undeflected. [3 marks]

subtopics.title: Induction
subtopics.syllabusContent: Magnetic flux Φ = BA cosθ. Faraday's law: ε = −NΔΦ/Δt. EMF in straight conductor: ε = BvL. Lenz's law and energy conservation. Sinusoidal EMF from rotating coil. Effect of changing rotation frequency.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Examples: time-varying magnetic fields; rotating coils; relative motion between conductor and field. Quantitative treatment limited to straight conductors at right angles and rectangular coils moving in/out of fields and rotating. Only qualitative treatment of self-induction. Inductance and RL circuits not required.
coreConcepts: Magnetic flux Φ = BA cosθ; maximum when B is perpendicular to the surface (θ = 0); zero when B is parallel to the surface.
Faraday's law: the magnitude of induced EMF equals the rate of change of flux linkage: |ε| = N|ΔΦ/Δt|.
Lenz's law: the induced EMF opposes the change in flux that causes it — this is a consequence of conservation of energy.
For a straight conductor of length L moving at speed v perpendicular to field B: ε = BvL.
A coil rotating with angular speed ω in uniform field B generates a sinusoidal EMF: ε = NBAω sin(ωt).
Increasing the rotation frequency of a generator increases both the peak EMF and its frequency.
Self-induction: a changing current in a coil induces an EMF in the same coil opposing the change — only qualitative treatment required.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking Lenz's law implies induced current always opposes the original current — it opposes the change in flux, not necessarily the original current direction.
Confusing magnetic flux with magnetic field strength — flux Φ = BA cosθ depends on area and angle as well as B.
Assuming the induced EMF is proportional to flux, not its rate of change — Faraday's law: EMF ∝ ΔΦ/Δt, not Φ itself.
Thinking that a coil at maximum flux (B perpendicular to surface) gives maximum EMF — at this position the rate of change of flux is zero, so EMF is zero.
Believing increasing rotation frequency of a generator only increases peak EMF — it also increases the frequency of the AC output.

conceptual: Explain Lenz's law and show how it is a consequence of conservation of energy.
Describe how a simple AC generator works, explaining why the output is sinusoidal.
Explain why the induced EMF is zero when a rotating coil is perpendicular to the magnetic field.
State Faraday's law of induction and explain the significance of the negative sign.
examStyle: A rectangular coil (N = 100, area = 0.02 m²) rotates at 50 Hz in a uniform field of 0.1 T. Calculate (i) the peak EMF, and (ii) the EMF when the plane of the coil makes 30° with the field. [5 marks]
A straight wire of length 0.5 m moves at 4 m/s perpendicular to a magnetic field of 0.3 T. Calculate the induced EMF and the current if the wire has resistance 2 Ω. [4 marks]
A bar magnet is dropped through a coil connected to a galvanometer. Sketch the galvanometer reading as a function of time and explain the shape of the graph using Faraday's and Lenz's laws. [5 marks]
Explain, using Faraday's law, why the EMF induced in a generator doubles when the frequency of rotation is doubled (assuming the same field and coil dimensions). [3 marks]

topics.title: Nuclear and quantum physics
topics.syllabusDescription: Atomic structure, quantum physics, radioactive decay, nuclear fission and fusion, and stellar evolution. Explores the quantum nature of matter and energy from atomic to cosmic scales.

subtopics.title: Structure of the atom
subtopics.syllabusContent: Geiger-Marsden-Rutherford experiment and nuclear model. Nuclear notation. Emission and absorption spectra: evidence for discrete energy levels. Photon emission and absorption E = hf. Nuclear radius R = R₀A^(1/3). Rutherford scattering deviations at high energy. Distance of closest approach. Bohr model energy levels En = −13.6/n² eV. Quantization of angular momentum.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Recall of chemical symbols not required. Qualitative approach to Geiger-Marsden-Rutherford at SL; quantitative at HL. Simple energy conservation for distance of closest approach. Energies low enough to consider only electric repulsion. Bohr model angular momentum quantization: mvr = nh/(2π).
coreConcepts: The Geiger-Marsden experiment (alpha particle scattering) showed that most of the atom is empty space with mass and positive charge concentrated in a tiny dense nucleus.
Nuclear notation: A/Z X where A = nucleon number, Z = proton number; number of neutrons N = A − Z.
Electrons in atoms occupy discrete energy levels; transitions between levels produce photons of specific frequencies: E = hf = E₂ − E₁.
Emission spectra: electrons fall to lower levels, emitting photons; absorption spectra: electrons absorb photons and move to higher levels.
Nuclear radius R = R₀A^(1/3) where R₀ ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m; nuclear density is approximately constant for all nuclei.
Bohr model for hydrogen: En = −13.6/n² eV; quantized angular momentum mvr = nh/(2π) restricts electrons to specific orbits.
Distance of closest approach: kinetic energy of alpha particle = electrostatic potential energy at closest approach: ½mv² = kq₁q₂/r.
At high energies, Rutherford scattering deviates from prediction as alpha particles reach the strong nuclear force range.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking that atoms are mostly solid material — they are mostly empty space; the nucleus is ~10⁻¹⁵ m compared with atomic diameter ~10⁻¹⁰ m.
Confusing emission and absorption spectra — emission produces bright lines on a dark background; absorption produces dark lines on a continuous spectrum at the same wavelengths.
Believing the Bohr model accurately describes all atoms — it works only for hydrogen-like (one-electron) systems; it fails for multi-electron atoms.
Assuming the Bohr model explains why electrons emit light — it postulates quantized orbits empirically; quantum mechanics provides the explanation.
Thinking nuclear density increases with nucleon number — since R ∝ A^(1/3), volume ∝ A, so nuclear density ρ = 3m_p/(4πR₀³) is approximately constant.

conceptual: Describe the Geiger-Marsden experiment and explain how the results led Rutherford to propose the nuclear model of the atom.
Explain how line emission spectra provide evidence for discrete energy levels in atoms.
Describe two features of high-energy alpha particle scattering that deviate from the Rutherford prediction and explain why.
State the two postulates of the Bohr model and explain how they lead to quantized energy levels.
examStyle: An alpha particle (mass 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) is fired at a gold nucleus (Z = 79) with kinetic energy 7.7 MeV. Calculate the distance of closest approach. [4 marks]
An electron in hydrogen transitions from n = 4 to n = 2. Calculate the energy and wavelength of the photon emitted. [5 marks]
Calculate the radius of a uranium-238 nucleus and the nuclear density. (R₀ = 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m, m_p = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) [5 marks]
Explain the difference between an emission spectrum and an absorption spectrum of hydrogen, and why they have dark/bright lines at the same wavelengths. [4 marks]

subtopics.title: Quantum physics
subtopics.syllabusContent: Photoelectric effect and particle nature of light. Threshold frequency. Work function and maximum kinetic energy: Emax = hf − Φ. Diffraction of particles: wave nature of matter. Wave-particle duality. De Broglie wavelength λ = h/p. Compton scattering: shift in wavelength Δλ = (h/mec)(1 − cosθ).
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Discussion of why photoelectric effect cannot be explained classically required. Scattering experiment with particle diffraction described. Compton formula derivation not required.
coreConcepts: The photoelectric effect: light below the threshold frequency ejects no electrons regardless of intensity; above threshold, the number of photoelectrons depends on intensity and their maximum kinetic energy depends on frequency.
Einstein's explanation: photons are quanta of light energy E = hf; a photon ejects an electron only if hf ≥ Φ (work function).
Maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons: Emax = hf − Φ; increasing intensity increases number of photoelectrons but not their maximum Ek.
Wave-particle duality: all matter and radiation exhibit both wave and particle properties depending on the experiment.
De Broglie wavelength λ = h/p = h/(mv); for macroscopic objects p is large, so λ is negligible — quantum effects not observed.
Electron diffraction confirms the wave nature of matter; the diffraction pattern is consistent with λ = h/p.
Compton scattering: an X-ray photon collides with a free electron, transferring momentum and energy; the scattered photon has a longer wavelength. Δλ = (h/mec)(1 − cosθ).
commonMisconceptions: Thinking brighter light (higher intensity) gives photoelectrons with more kinetic energy — intensity determines number of photoelectrons; kinetic energy depends only on frequency.
Believing any frequency of light can cause the photoelectric effect given sufficient intensity — no; frequency must exceed the threshold frequency regardless of intensity.
Confusing photon energy with photon momentum — E = hf; p = h/λ = hf/c; both are quantized properties of the photon.
Thinking de Broglie wavelength only applies to electrons — it applies to all matter including protons, neutrons, and even large molecules.
Assuming Compton scattering is the same as the photoelectric effect — in Compton scattering the photon is not absorbed; it is scattered with reduced energy (longer wavelength).

conceptual: Explain why the classical wave model of light fails to account for the photoelectric effect, and how Einstein's photon model resolves each difficulty.
Describe what is meant by wave-particle duality and give one example of evidence for the wave nature of particles and one for the particle nature of waves.
Explain why Compton scattering provides stronger evidence for the particle nature of light than the photoelectric effect.
Explain why quantum effects such as diffraction are not observable for macroscopic objects using the de Broglie hypothesis.
examStyle: Light of wavelength 250 nm illuminates a metal surface with work function 4.5 eV. Calculate (i) the photon energy in eV, (ii) the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons, and (iii) the threshold wavelength. [6 marks]
An electron is accelerated through 5000 V. Calculate its de Broglie wavelength. (m_e = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg) [5 marks]
An X-ray photon of wavelength 0.020 nm undergoes Compton scattering at θ = 90°. Calculate the wavelength of the scattered photon and the kinetic energy gained by the electron. [5 marks]
Describe an experiment that demonstrates electron diffraction and explain how it confirms wave-particle duality. [4 marks]

subtopics.title: Radioactive decay
subtopics.syllabusContent: Isotopes. Nuclear binding energy and mass defect. Binding energy per nucleon variation. E = mc². Strong nuclear force. Random and spontaneous decay. Alpha, beta-minus, beta-plus and gamma decay equations. Neutrinos and antineutrinos. Penetration and ionization. Activity, count rate, half-life. Decay law N = N₀e^(−λt). Activity A = λN. Half-life T₁/₂ = ln2/λ.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Nuclear masses in kg, MeVc⁻² and u. Contexts: medical isotopes, leak detection, thickness gauging, radioactive dating. Weak nuclear force not considered. Exponential decay law required for HL. Half-life determination required.
coreConcepts: Nuclear binding energy = mass defect × c²; the mass of a nucleus is always less than the sum of its constituents' masses.
Binding energy per nucleon peaks around iron-56 (A ≈ 56); nuclei below this gain energy by fusion; above this by fission.
The strong nuclear force is short-range (~10⁻¹⁵ m), attractive between nucleons, and overcomes electrostatic repulsion within the nucleus.
Alpha decay: A/Z X → A−4/(Z−2) Y + ⁴₂He; beta-minus: ¹/₀n → ¹/₁p + ⁰/₋₁e + antineutrino; beta-plus: ¹/₁p → ¹/₀n + ⁰/₁e + neutrino.
Radioactive decay is random (cannot predict which nucleus decays) and spontaneous (not affected by external conditions).
Activity A = λN; decay law: N = N₀e^(−λt); half-life T₁/₂ = ln2/λ.

Alpha particles have high ionizing power but low penetration (stopped by paper); beta particles moderate ionization/penetration (stopped by a few mm of aluminium); gamma rays low ionization but high penetration (reduced by lead/thick concrete).
