The continuous spectrum of beta decay energies provided evidence for the existence of the neutrino (energy and momentum conservation).
commonMisconceptions: Thinking radioactive decay can be controlled by temperature, pressure or chemical state — it is spontaneous and unaffected by external physical conditions.
Confusing activity with count rate — count rate depends on detector geometry and efficiency; activity is the actual rate of decay.
Assuming all radiation types have the same penetration and ionization — alpha, beta and gamma have very different penetrating and ionizing abilities.
Thinking half-life is the time for all radioactive material to decay — it is the time for half the remaining nuclei to decay; theoretically some atoms always remain.
Confusing mass defect and binding energy — mass defect is the difference in mass; binding energy is the equivalent energy (ΔE = Δm × c²).
Believing the most tightly bound nucleus is the heaviest — iron-56 has the maximum binding energy per nucleon, not the heaviest nuclei.

conceptual: Explain why the binding energy per nucleon peaks at around iron-56 and what this implies for both fission and fusion as energy sources.
Explain what is meant by radioactive decay being 'random and spontaneous' and why this makes exact predictions for individual nuclei impossible.
Describe the evidence from beta decay that led to the prediction of the neutrino.
Compare the penetrating and ionizing properties of alpha, beta and gamma radiation and explain their practical implications.
examStyle: Radium-226 has a half-life of 1600 years. A sample initially contains 8 × 10²⁰ atoms. Calculate (i) the decay constant, (ii) the initial activity, and (iii) the number of atoms remaining after 4800 years. [6 marks]
Calculate the binding energy per nucleon of helium-4 (mass = 4.00260 u) given: proton mass = 1.00728 u, neutron mass = 1.00867 u. (1 u = 931.5 MeVc⁻²) [5 marks]
Write the complete nuclear equation for (i) the alpha decay of ²²⁶₈₈Ra, (ii) the beta-minus decay of ¹⁴₆C, and (iii) the beta-plus decay of ²²₁₁Na. [6 marks]
A radioactive source has activity 1.2 × 10⁵ Bq at t = 0 and 3.0 × 10⁴ Bq at t = 40 minutes. Calculate the half-life and the decay constant. [5 marks]

subtopics.title: Fission
subtopics.syllabusContent: Energy released in spontaneous and neutron-induced fission. Chain reactions. Control rods, moderators, heat exchangers and shielding in nuclear power plants. Properties and management of fission products.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Calculations of energy released in fission required. Long-term management of nuclear waste considered. Impact of nuclear waste storage discussed.
coreConcepts: Fission releases energy because the products have greater binding energy per nucleon than the original heavy nucleus — the mass defect is converted to energy via E = mc².
Neutron-induced fission: a slow (thermal) neutron is absorbed by a heavy nucleus (e.g., U-235), producing unstable nucleus that splits into two smaller nuclei plus additional neutrons and energy.
Chain reaction: the neutrons released trigger further fissions; if on average ≥1 neutron per fission causes another fission (critical), the reaction sustains itself.
Control rods (e.g., boron) absorb neutrons to regulate the chain reaction; moderators (e.g., water, graphite) slow fast neutrons to thermal energies for more efficient absorption.
Heat exchangers transfer thermal energy from the reactor coolant to produce steam for turbines; shielding (concrete, lead) protects against radiation.
Fission products are typically radioactive with long half-lives, requiring safe, long-term storage (hundreds to thousands of years) in geological repositories.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking nuclear reactors can explode like nuclear bombs — reactors have much lower enrichment levels of fissile material and engineered safety systems that prevent explosive chain reactions.
Assuming all neutrons produced in fission immediately cause more fissions — fast neutrons are less likely to cause fission in U-235; moderators slow them to thermal energies for efficient absorption.
Confusing control rods with the moderator — control rods absorb neutrons to control reaction rate; the moderator slows neutrons without absorbing them.
Thinking nuclear waste is only hazardous for a few years — some isotopes have half-lives of thousands to millions of years.
Believing fission violates conservation of mass-energy — mass decreases and energy is released; total mass-energy is conserved.

conceptual: Explain why neutron-induced fission of U-235 releases energy, using the concept of binding energy per nucleon.
Describe the roles of the moderator and control rods in a nuclear reactor and explain why they are separate components.
Discuss the environmental considerations in the long-term management of nuclear waste from fission reactors.
Explain the conditions needed for a self-sustaining chain reaction and distinguish between subcritical, critical and supercritical states.
examStyle: In a fission reaction, U-235 splits to form Ba-141 and Kr-92 plus neutrons. Calculate (i) the number of neutrons released, (ii) the mass defect in u, and (iii) the energy released per fission in MeV. [6 marks]
A reactor produces 500 MW of electrical power with 35% efficiency. Calculate the number of fission events per second required, assuming 200 MeV is released per fission. [5 marks]
Explain why slow (thermal) neutrons are more effective than fast neutrons at inducing fission in U-235 and describe how a moderator achieves this. [4 marks]

subtopics.title: Fusion and stars
subtopics.syllabusContent: Stellar equilibrium: radiation pressure vs gravitational force. Fusion as stellar energy source. Conditions for fusion (density and temperature). Effect of stellar mass on evolution. Hertzsprung-Russell diagram. Stellar parallax d = 1/p (parsec, arcsecond). Determination of stellar radii.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Energy release calculations required. Conversion between AU, ly and parsec required. HR diagram: main sequence, red giants, supergiants, white dwarfs, instability strip, lines of constant radius. Luminosity on vertical axis, temperature on horizontal axis (decreasing). Surface temperature and composition from stellar spectrum. Stellar radii from luminosity and temperature. Cepheid variables not required.
coreConcepts: Stars are in equilibrium when outward radiation pressure (from fusion) balances inward gravitational force; when fuel runs out, this balance is disrupted.
Fusion releases energy because combining light nuclei produces products with greater binding energy per nucleon; mass defect is converted to energy.
Fusion requires extreme temperatures (T ~ 10⁷ K) and densities for protons to overcome electrostatic repulsion and reach the range of the strong nuclear force.
Stellar mass determines the evolutionary path: low-mass stars become red giants then white dwarfs; high-mass stars become supergiants then neutron stars or black holes.
The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram plots luminosity vs temperature; the main sequence runs from hot-luminous to cool-dim; red giants are bright and cool; white dwarfs are dim and hot.
Stellar parallax: d (parsec) = 1/p (arcsecond); valid for stars within ~100 pc; 1 pc ≈ 3.26 ly ≈ 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m.
Stefan-Boltzmann law links luminosity, radius and temperature: L = 4πR²σT⁴; given L and T, stellar radius R can be determined.
Surface temperature of a star is determined from its spectrum (peak wavelength via Wien's law) and its chemical composition from spectral absorption lines.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking fusion is easier to achieve than fission — fusion requires overcoming enormous electrostatic repulsion and needs extreme conditions; fission with thermal neutrons is easier to initiate.
Assuming all stars evolve the same way — stellar mass is the primary factor; low-mass stars become white dwarfs while high-mass stars may explode as supernovae.
Confusing the x-axis direction on HR diagrams — temperature decreases from left to right; hot stars are on the left.
Thinking parallax angle is the angle subtended by the star — it is the angle subtended by the Earth-Sun distance as seen from the star (half of the total apparent shift).
Believing luminosity and brightness are the same — luminosity is intrinsic total power output; apparent brightness also depends on distance from the observer.
Confusing white dwarfs and neutron stars on the HR diagram — white dwarfs are hot and dim (bottom left); neutron stars are too small to appear significantly on standard HR diagrams.

conceptual: Explain why stars require such extreme temperatures and densities for fusion to occur.
Describe the life cycle of a star with mass similar to the Sun from main sequence to its end state, using the HR diagram.
Explain how the Stefan-Boltzmann law and Wien's displacement law together allow the radius of a star to be determined from observations.
Compare nuclear fusion and fission as energy sources, discussing the binding energy per nucleon curve.
examStyle: A star has luminosity 4L⊙ and surface temperature 10000 K. Given L⊙ = 3.85 × 10²⁶ W and the Sun's surface temperature is 5800 K, calculate the radius of this star. [5 marks]
A star has a parallax angle of 0.25 arcseconds. Calculate its distance in (i) parsecs, (ii) light years, and (iii) metres. [4 marks]
Calculate the energy released in the following fusion reaction: ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n. (Masses: ²H = 2.01410 u, ³H = 3.01605 u, ⁴He = 4.00260 u, n = 1.00867 u; 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c²) [5 marks]
Sketch an HR diagram and mark the approximate positions of: (i) the Sun, (ii) a red giant, (iii) a white dwarf, and (iv) a blue supergiant. Label the axes correctly. [5 marks]

subjects.name: Computer Science
assessmentObjectives: AO3 Constructing, analysing, evaluating and formulating
AO4 Using skills for effective problem-solving

topics.title: Systems in organizations
topics.syllabusDescription: Planning, installation, operation and maintenance of information systems in organizational contexts, including change management, documentation, training and backup.

subtopics.title: Identify the context for which a new system is planned
subtopics.syllabusContent: Identify the context for which a new system is planned, including the organizational setting, users, existing processes and technologies, and constraints.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: The extent and limitations of a new system should be appreciated. Organizational issues related to the installation of new systems such as user roles and underlying technologies should be considered.
coreConcepts: New systems must be planned with a clear understanding of the organizational context and constraints.
Existing processes and technologies influence feasible design choices.
Different user roles may have different expectations and requirements for a new system.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming a system can be designed in isolation from existing processes.
Ignoring limitations such as budget, technology and organizational policies.
Thinking that user roles do not significantly affect system requirements.

conceptual: Identify the context for which a new point-of-sale system is planned in a supermarket.
Describe two contextual factors that might affect the design of a school learning management system.
examStyle: A small business is planning a new inventory system. Identify two aspects of the context that the analyst should investigate.
Describe three constraints that an analyst must consider when planning a new library management system.

subtopics.title: Describe the need for change management
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Describe the need for change management.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Describe why change management is needed when new systems are introduced, including planning, communication, training and support.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should understand there are a number of factors that need to be managed to ensure change is successful.
coreConcepts: Change management coordinates technical and human factors to ensure successful system adoption.
Poorly managed change can result in user resistance, productivity loss and project failure.
Effective communication and training help users adapt to new systems.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming that installing the software is sufficient for successful change.
Overlooking user training and ongoing support.
Believing that users will automatically accept and use the new system.

conceptual: Describe two reasons why change management is important when implementing a new payroll system.
Explain how poor change management can affect employee productivity.
examStyle: A hospital is introducing a new patient records system. Describe the need for change management in this context.
Explain two strategies that management could use to reduce user resistance when introducing a new enterprise resource planning (ERP) system.

subtopics.title: Outline compatibility issues resulting from legacy systems and mergers
subtopics.syllabusContent: Outline technical and organizational compatibility issues that can arise when integrating or replacing systems, particularly with legacy systems or after business mergers.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: When organizations interact, particularly on an international basis, there may be issues of software compatibility and language differences.
coreConcepts: Legacy systems may use outdated hardware, software and data formats that are difficult to integrate.
Business mergers may require integrating heterogeneous systems with different standards and languages.
Compatibility issues can affect interoperability, data exchange and user workflows.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming that new software will automatically work with legacy systems.
Ignoring language and localization issues in international organizations.
Believing that compatibility problems can be solved without cost or disruption.

conceptual: Outline one compatibility issue that may arise when merging two companies that use different database systems.
Outline one compatibility issue that can occur when connecting a legacy system to a modern web service.
examStyle: A multinational company acquires a smaller firm that uses a legacy accounting system. Outline two compatibility issues that may arise.
Outline two compatibility issues that could arise when two banks with different legacy systems merge their IT infrastructure.

subtopics.title: Compare implementing systems on client hardware vs remote hosting
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Compare the implementation of systems using a client’s hardware with hosting systems remotely.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Compare running systems on client-owned hardware with using remotely hosted solutions such as Software-as-a-Service.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: The benefits and drawbacks of SaaS (Software-as-a-Service) should be considered. The remote host may be in a different time zone and this can have significant effects on end-users.
coreConcepts: On-premises solutions offer more direct control and potentially higher customization but require higher capital and maintenance costs.
Remote hosting and SaaS can reduce infrastructure costs and simplify updates but depend on network connectivity and provider reliability.
Geographical and time zone differences may influence performance, support and maintenance windows.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming that cloud solutions are always cheaper and better.
Ignoring data protection and compliance issues when using remote hosting.
Believing that on-premises hosting eliminates all security risks.

conceptual: Compare two advantages of using a SaaS solution instead of an on-premises system.
Compare one social and one ethical issue related to hosting systems remotely.
examStyle: An organization is deciding whether to install a customer relationship management (CRM) system on its own servers or to use a remotely hosted SaaS solution. Compare these two options.
Discuss the implications of hosting a school's student information system on a remote server located in a different time zone.

subtopics.title: Evaluate alternative installation processes
subtopics.syllabusContent: Evaluate parallel running, pilot running, direct changeover and phased conversion as methods for installing new systems.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should be aware of the methods of implementation/conversion. Training issues may require organizations to restructure their workforce.
coreConcepts: Different installation methods balance risk, cost, speed and complexity.
Parallel running reduces risk but increases cost and workload.
Direct changeover is quick but risky if problems appear after go-live.
Pilot and phased approaches limit risk by reducing the scope of change.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming direct changeover is always the best because it is fastest.
Underestimating time and resources needed for parallel or phased approaches.
Ignoring user training and support requirements in choosing an installation method.

conceptual: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using parallel running when installing a new information system.
Explain why pilot running might be chosen for a national government system.
examStyle: Evaluate the use of direct changeover and phased conversion for implementing a new airline reservation system.
Compare parallel running and pilot running as installation methods for a new national tax-filing system.

subtopics.title: Discuss problems that may arise as part of data migration
subtopics.syllabusContent: Discuss problems that can occur when transferring data between systems, including incompatible file formats, structures, validation rules, incomplete transfers and international conventions.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: These include incompatible file formats, data structures, validation rules, incomplete data transfer and international conventions on dates, currencies and character sets.
coreConcepts: Data migration is prone to errors that can compromise data integrity and completeness.
Differences in data formats, structures and validation rules can cause data loss or corruption.
International conventions on dates, currencies and characters must be handled carefully.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking data migration is simply copying files between systems.
Ignoring the need for validation and verification after migration.
Assuming that different systems use the same date and currency formats.

conceptual: Discuss two problems that may arise when migrating customer data from one database system to another.
Explain why international date formats can cause problems during data migration.
examStyle: A company is moving its payroll data from an old system to a new one. Discuss problems that may arise during this migration.
Discuss two problems related to international conventions on dates and currencies that may occur when migrating data from a UK-based system to a US-based system.

subtopics.title: Suggest various types of testing
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Suggest various types of testing.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Suggest different types of testing at various stages, including user acceptance testing, debugging and beta testing, and automated testing.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: The crucial importance of testing at all stages of implementation should be emphasized, with the stages clearly defined. Students should be aware that there are programs that can test other programs.
coreConcepts: Testing is necessary throughout development and implementation to detect and correct defects.
Different kinds of testing focus on different aspects of system quality and reliability.
Automated tests can reduce cost and improve consistency in large systems.
commonMisconceptions: Believing that testing can be left to the end of development.
Assuming that one type of testing is sufficient for all purposes.
Confusing debugging with formal testing.

conceptual: Suggest two types of testing that should be carried out before deploying a new web-based system.
Describe how automated testing tools can be used in software development.
examStyle: Suggest three different types of testing that could be used when developing a new online banking system.
Describe the difference between user acceptance testing and beta testing, and explain when each should be carried out.

subtopics.title: Describe the importance of user documentation
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Describe the importance of user documentation.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Describe why user documentation is important for helping end-users understand and use a system effectively.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: The quality of user documentation can affect the rate of implementation of the new system.
coreConcepts: User documentation supports users in learning and using a system.
Good documentation can reduce support costs and speed up adoption.
Poor documentation can lead to errors, frustration and reduced productivity.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming that users will not read documentation and so it is not important.
Believing that documentation only needs to cover basic features.
Ignoring different user skill levels and accessibility needs.

conceptual: Describe two reasons why user documentation is important for a new accounting system.
Explain how good user documentation can reduce support costs.
examStyle: Describe the importance of user documentation for an online ticket booking system.
Explain how poor user documentation could negatively affect the successful adoption of a new hospital management system.

subtopics.title: Evaluate different methods of providing user documentation
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Evaluate different methods of providing user documentation.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Evaluate methods of providing user documentation such as help files, online support and printed manuals.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Examples should include methods such as help files, online support and printed manuals.
coreConcepts: Different documentation formats have different strengths for different users and contexts.
Online documentation can be updated easily but requires network access.
Printed manuals can be more accessible in some environments but may become outdated.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming online help always replaces the need for printed material.
Ignoring users with limited internet connectivity.
Believing that a single documentation method will suit all users.

conceptual: Evaluate using only online help files as user documentation for a school information system.
Compare printed manuals and context-sensitive help in terms of usability.
examStyle: Evaluate different methods of providing user documentation for a new productivity application.
Compare context-sensitive help files and printed manuals as methods of user documentation for elderly users of a government benefits portal.

subtopics.title: Evaluate different methods of delivering user training
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Evaluate different methods of delivering user training.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Evaluate methods of delivering user training such as self-instruction, formal classes and remote/online training.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Examples should include self instruction, formal classes, remote/online training. The quality of the delivery of user training can affect the rate of implementation of the new system.
coreConcepts: Training methods vary in cost, flexibility and effectiveness for different learners.
Self-instruction can be cost-effective but may not suit all learning styles.
Formal classes and remote training can provide structure and interaction but require scheduling and resources.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming that users will learn the system without formal training.
Believing that online training is always superior or cheaper.
Ignoring the need for ongoing training when systems change.

conceptual: Evaluate self-instruction as a training method for office workers when a new email client is installed.
Discuss advantages and disadvantages of online training for geographically dispersed staff.
examStyle: Evaluate different methods of delivering user training for a new hospital information system.
Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using online remote training to train staff in a large retail chain on a new point-of-sale system.

subtopics.title: Identify a range of causes of data loss
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Identify a range of causes of data loss.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Identify various causes of data loss including malicious activities and natural disasters.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Causes include malicious activities and natural disasters. Malicious activity may be a result of activities by employees within the organization or intruders.
coreConcepts: Data can be lost due to technical failures, human actions and external events.
Malicious activity can originate from both inside and outside an organization.
Understanding causes of data loss helps in designing appropriate prevention strategies.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking that only external attackers cause data loss.
Ignoring physical threats such as fire or flood.
Assuming cloud storage eliminates the risk of data loss.

conceptual: Identify two causes of data loss that may affect a small business.
Outline one malicious and one non-malicious cause of data loss.
examStyle: Identify four possible causes of data loss in an organization.
Outline two ways in which employees within an organization could cause data loss and suggest one preventative measure for each.

subtopics.title: Outline the consequences of data loss in a specified situation
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Outline the consequences of data loss in a specified situation.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Outline possible consequences of data loss for different kinds of organizations and systems.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Examples include loss of medical records or cancellation of a hotel reservation without the knowledge of the traveller.
coreConcepts: Data loss can have serious operational, financial, legal and reputational consequences.
The severity of consequences depends on the type of data and the context.
Critical systems such as healthcare or transport can have life-threatening consequences if data is lost.
commonMisconceptions: Underestimating long-term effects of data loss on trust and reputation.
Assuming that data can always be easily reconstructed.
Believing that only large organizations experience serious consequences.

conceptual: Outline the consequences of data loss for a hospital storing patient records electronically.
Describe one consequence of data loss for an airline reservation system.
examStyle: In the context of an online hotel booking system, outline three consequences of data loss for customers.
Describe two consequences of data loss for a bank that stores customer transaction records electronically.

subtopics.title: Describe methods that can be used to prevent data loss
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Describe a range of methods that can be used to prevent data loss.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Describe methods used to prevent or reduce data loss, including failover systems, redundancy, removable media and offsite/online storage.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: These should include failover systems, redundancy, removable media, offsite/online storage.
coreConcepts: Data protection strategies aim to reduce the likelihood and impact of data loss.
Redundancy and failover systems provide alternative copies and paths when components fail.
Regular backups to removable or offsite storage support recovery after major incidents.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming a single backup is sufficient protection.
Ignoring the need to test recovery procedures.
Believing that cloud storage does not need its own backup strategy.

conceptual: Describe two methods that can be used to prevent data loss in a small company.
Explain how redundancy can help to prevent data loss.
examStyle: Describe three methods that an organization can use to prevent data loss.
Explain how a failover system can help an organization recover from an unexpected server failure.

subtopics.title: Describe strategies for managing releases and updates
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Describe strategies for managing releases and updates.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Describe strategies for managing software releases and updates, including patches, service packs and automatic updates.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should be aware of a variety of ways in which updates and patches are made available and deployed. This includes automatic updates received on a regular basis online.
coreConcepts: Software releases and updates must be managed to maintain security, stability and compatibility.
Automatic updates can improve security but may disrupt users or cause compatibility issues.
Organizations may use staged or scheduled deployment to reduce risk.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming updates always improve systems without risk.
Ignoring the impact of updates on older hardware or software.
Believing that users can safely ignore updates indefinitely.

conceptual: Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of automatic software updates for home users.
Explain why organizations may choose to delay installing some updates.
examStyle: Describe two strategies an organization could use to manage software releases and updates across hundreds of client computers.
Discuss the risks to an organization of automatically applying software updates immediately across all client computers without prior testing.

topics.title: System design basics
topics.syllabusDescription: Basic concepts of computer systems, system design and analysis, and human interaction with systems.

subtopics.title: Define hardware, software, peripheral, network, human resources
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Define the terms: hardware, software, peripheral, network, human resources.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Define basic components of a computer system and its environment: hardware, software, peripheral, network and human resources.
coreConcepts: Hardware refers to the physical components of a computer system.
Software refers to the programs and instructions that run on hardware.
Peripherals are external devices that provide input, output or storage.
A network connects multiple devices to share resources.
Human resources refers to the people who operate, manage and maintain the system.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing software with the data it processes.
Thinking that all external devices are part of the core system rather than peripherals.
Ignoring the role of people as part of a computer system.

conceptual: Define the term hardware.
Define the term peripheral.
examStyle: Define the terms software and network.
Identify one example each of hardware, software, a peripheral, a network, and a human resource found in a typical school computer lab.

subtopics.title: Describe roles that a computer can take in a networked world
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Describe the roles that a computer can take in a networked world.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Describe different roles computers can take in a networked environment, such as client, server, email server, DNS server, router and firewall.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Roles include client, server, email server, DNS server, router and firewall.
coreConcepts: Clients request services and resources from servers.
Servers provide services such as web, email or file storage to clients.
Routers direct data packets between networks.
Firewalls control traffic to enforce security policies.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming any computer can act as a server without configuration.
Confusing routers with switches or hubs.
Believing that firewalls completely prevent all security breaches.

conceptual: Describe the role of a DNS server.
Describe the role of a router in a home network.
examStyle: Describe two different roles that computers can have in a networked environment.
Explain the difference between the roles of a web server and a DNS server in handling a user's request to visit a website.

subtopics.title: Discuss social and ethical issues associated with a networked world
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Discuss the social and ethical issues associated with a networked world.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Discuss social and ethical issues arising from widespread networking and connectivity, such as privacy, security, digital divide and impact on behaviour.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Develop an appreciation of the social and ethical issues associated with continued developments in computer systems.
coreConcepts: Networking enables global communication and access to information but raises privacy and security concerns.
Access to networked resources is uneven, creating a digital divide.
Ethical issues include misuse of data, cybercrime and the impact on social interaction.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming network access is equally available to everyone.
Believing that data on networks is always secure.
Ignoring ethical responsibilities when sharing or using digital content.

conceptual: Discuss how a networked world can contribute to the digital divide.
Discuss one social and one ethical issue associated with social networking sites.
examStyle: Discuss the social and ethical issues associated with the increasing use of wireless networks in public spaces.
Evaluate the impact of the digital divide on students in developing countries who rely on networked learning resources.

subtopics.title: Identify relevant stakeholders when planning a new system
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Identify the relevant stakeholders when planning a new system.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Identify stakeholders who should be considered when planning a new system, including end-users, management, developers and others affected.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: The role of the end-user must be considered when planning a new system. Who is a relevant stakeholder?
coreConcepts: Stakeholders are individuals or groups who are affected by or can affect a system.
End-users are critical stakeholders whose needs must be understood.
Ignoring stakeholders can lead to systems that do not meet real requirements.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming that only management and IT staff are stakeholders.
Ignoring external stakeholders such as customers or regulatory bodies.
Believing that all stakeholders have the same priorities.

conceptual: Identify two stakeholders when planning a new school attendance system.
Identify three stakeholders in the development of an online shopping site.
examStyle: Identify four relevant stakeholders when planning a new hospital appointment system.
Describe why end-users are considered one of the most important stakeholders when planning a new mobile banking application.

subtopics.title: Describe methods of obtaining requirements from stakeholders
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Describe methods of obtaining requirements from stakeholders.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Describe methods for obtaining requirements such as surveys, interviews and direct observations.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Including surveys, interviews, direct observations. The need for effective collaboration to obtain appropriate information from stakeholders.
coreConcepts: Requirements can be gathered using a variety of techniques, each with strengths and weaknesses.
Surveys can reach many stakeholders but may lack depth.
Interviews and observations can provide detailed insights but are time-consuming.
commonMisconceptions: Relying on a single method of requirements gathering.
Assuming that stakeholders always express their needs clearly.
Ignoring privacy concerns when observing or recording users.

conceptual: Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of using interviews to obtain system requirements.
Explain why direct observation can be useful when gathering requirements.
examStyle: Describe two methods that a systems analyst could use to obtain requirements from stakeholders for a new payroll system.
Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using direct observation to gather requirements for a new warehouse management system.

subtopics.title: Describe techniques for gathering information for a workable solution
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Describe appropriate techniques for gathering the information needed to arrive at a workable solution.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Describe techniques for gathering information about current systems, competing products, organizational capabilities and literature.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Examining current systems, competing products, organizational capabilities, literature searches.
coreConcepts: Understanding current systems and competing products helps to identify requirements and constraints.
Organizational capabilities, such as skills and resources, influence feasible solutions.
Literature and documentation provide best practices and existing solutions.
commonMisconceptions: Ignoring existing systems and starting design from scratch.
Assuming that a solution used by another organization will work unchanged.
Failing to consider limitations in organizational skills or resources.

conceptual: Describe how examining competing products can help in the design of a new system.
Describe why organizational capabilities must be considered when proposing a solution.
examStyle: Describe two techniques that can be used to gather information about existing systems before designing a replacement.
Explain why examining competing products is a valuable technique when gathering information for the design of a new e-commerce platform.

subtopics.title: Construct representations to illustrate system requirements
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Construct suitable representations to illustrate system requirements.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Construct representations such as system flow charts, data flow diagrams and structure charts to show system requirements.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Examples include: system flow charts, data flow diagrams, structure chart. UML is not required.
coreConcepts: Graphical representations help to communicate system requirements and design.
System flow charts show the overall flow of data and control.
Data flow diagrams focus on the movement and transformation of data.
Structure charts represent the decomposition of a system into modules.
commonMisconceptions: Mixing different diagram types without clear notation.
Assuming diagrams are only documentation and not part of analysis.
Overcomplicating diagrams so that they are hard to read.

conceptual: Construct a simple system flow chart to show the processing of online orders.
Draw a data flow diagram to illustrate how student data is collected and stored in a school system.
examStyle: Construct a system flow chart to represent the process of issuing and returning books in a library management system.
Draw a data flow diagram to represent the process of a student submitting an assignment through an online learning platform.

subtopics.title: Describe the purpose of prototypes
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Describe the purpose of prototypes to demonstrate the proposed system to the client.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Describe how prototypes are used to demonstrate and refine proposed systems with clients.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Prototypes help gather information to resolve complex problems and support logical and critical thinking.
coreConcepts: Prototypes provide an early, simplified version of a system to gather feedback.
They help clarify requirements and identify usability issues.
Prototypes reduce risk by allowing changes before full development.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing prototypes with final systems.
Believing that building prototypes always increases development time.
Ignoring feedback gathered from prototype evaluation.

conceptual: Describe the purpose of using a prototype when developing a new mobile application.
Explain why a prototype can help communicate ideas to a client.
examStyle: Describe two reasons why a prototype might be used during the design of a new reservation system.
Explain how a prototype can help resolve misunderstandings between a client and a developer during the design of a new mobile app.

subtopics.title: Discuss the importance of iteration during the design process
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Discuss the importance of iteration during the design process.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Discuss why design processes often involve repeated cycles of design, implementation and evaluation.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Linked to iterative design models such as the design cycle.
coreConcepts: Iteration allows designers to refine solutions based on feedback and testing.
Early designs rarely meet all requirements perfectly.
Iterative design reduces risk by addressing problems progressively.
commonMisconceptions: Believing that a single pass through the design process is sufficient.
Confusing iteration with rework due to poor planning.
Assuming iteration is only needed for large projects.

conceptual: Discuss the importance of iteration in improving the usability of a system.
Explain how iteration can reduce risk in system development.
examStyle: Discuss the importance of iteration during the design of an online banking system.
Discuss two advantages of using an iterative design process compared to completing each design stage only once.

subtopics.title: Explain consequences of failing to involve end-users in the design process
subtopics.syllabusContent: Explain consequences such as systems that do not meet user needs, reduced productivity and resistance to change when end-users are not involved.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: The failure to involve the end user may lead to software that is not suitable for its intended use, which may have adverse effects on user productivity.
coreConcepts: End-user involvement helps ensure that systems meet real needs and workflows.
Failing to involve end-users can lead to poor usability and rejection of the system.
User dissatisfaction can reduce productivity and increase support costs.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming that developers alone can define user needs.
Believing that involving users will slow down the project without benefit.
Ignoring feedback from early user testing.

conceptual: Explain two consequences of failing to involve teachers in the design of a school grading system.
Explain why end-user involvement is important when designing a medical records system.
examStyle: Explain the possible consequences of failing to involve end-users in the design process of a new airline check-in system.
Explain two consequences that may result from failing to involve end-users during the testing phase of a new system.

subtopics.title: Discuss social and ethical issues of introducing new IT systems
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Discuss the social and ethical issues associated with the introduction of new IT systems.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Discuss social and ethical issues that arise when new IT systems are introduced, including job changes, privacy, security and environmental impact.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Develop an appreciation of the social and ethical issues associated with continued developments in specified computer systems.
coreConcepts: New IT systems can change working patterns, require new skills and displace some jobs.
Privacy and security concerns increase when more data is collected and processed.
Environmental impacts include energy use and e-waste.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming new IT systems only bring benefits.
Ignoring the need for policies to govern data use.
Believing social and ethical issues are purely technical problems.

conceptual: Discuss two social issues associated with introducing automated checkout systems in supermarkets.
Discuss one ethical and one environmental issue related to cloud computing.
examStyle: Discuss the social and ethical issues associated with introducing an automated attendance monitoring system in schools.
Explain two ethical issues that an organization must consider when introducing an automated employee monitoring system.

subtopics.title: Define the term usability
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Define the term usability.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Define usability in the context of human–computer interaction, including effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: This includes ergonomics and accessibility.
coreConcepts: Usability refers to how effectively, efficiently and satisfactorily users can achieve goals with a system.
Ergonomics and accessibility are aspects of usability.
Good usability reduces errors and user frustration.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing usability with only aesthetic appearance.
Ignoring accessibility as part of usability.
Assuming usability is subjective and cannot be evaluated.

conceptual: Define the term usability.
Define the term accessibility in the context of computer systems.
examStyle: Define usability.
Explain why usability is an important consideration when designing a system for use by non-technical users.

subtopics.title: Identify usability problems with commonly used digital devices
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Identify a range of usability problems with commonly used digital devices.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Identify usability problems in devices such as PCs, digital cameras, cell phones, game consoles and media players.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should be aware of usability issues in a range of devices including PCs, digital cameras, cell phones, games consoles, MP3 players and other commonly used digital devices.
coreConcepts: Common devices may have usability issues such as complex navigation or unclear feedback.
Different user groups may experience usability problems differently.
Identifying problems is a first step towards improving design.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming popular devices have perfect usability.
Focusing only on visual design rather than interaction.
Ignoring the needs of users with disabilities.

conceptual: Identify two usability problems associated with mobile phones for elderly users.
Identify one usability problem for each of the following: digital cameras and game consoles.
examStyle: Identify four usability problems that may arise when using a small portable media player.
Identify two usability problems that elderly users may experience when interacting with a smartphone touchscreen interface.

subtopics.title: Identify methods to improve accessibility of systems
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Identify methods that can be used to improve the accessibility of systems.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Identify methods such as touch screens, voice recognition, text-to-speech and Braille keyboards to improve accessibility.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Examples include touch screen, voice recognition, text-to-speech, Braille keyboard.
coreConcepts: Accessible systems support users with different abilities.
Assistive technologies help overcome sensory or motor limitations.
Designing for accessibility can improve usability for all users.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming accessibility features are only needed for a small number of users.
Believing accessibility always increases cost and complexity.
Ignoring accessibility in early stages of design.

conceptual: Identify two methods that can improve accessibility of a website.
Describe one way in which voice recognition can improve accessibility.
examStyle: Identify four methods that can be used to improve the accessibility of computer systems for users with visual impairments.
Describe two methods that can be used to improve the accessibility of a website for users with hearing impairments.

subtopics.title: Identify usability problems that can occur in a system
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Identify a range of usability problems that can occur in a system.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Identify usability problems in systems such as ticketing, online payroll, scheduling, voice recognition and feedback systems.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: These should be related to systems such as ticketing, online payroll, scheduling, voice recognition and systems that provide feedback.
coreConcepts: Usability problems in complex systems can affect accuracy, speed and user satisfaction.
Examples include confusing interfaces, unclear error messages and slow response times.
Recognizing these problems supports redesign and improvement.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming business systems are always usable because they are widely deployed.
Focusing only on functional correctness rather than user experience.
Ignoring the effect of context, such as stress or time pressure, on usability.

conceptual: Identify two usability problems that might occur in an online ticketing system.
Identify two usability problems associated with automated voice recognition customer support systems.
examStyle: Identify four usability problems that may occur in an online payroll system.
Describe two usability problems that could occur when a medical professional uses a complex hospital records system under time pressure.

subtopics.title: Discuss implications of human–machine interaction
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Discuss the moral, ethical, social, economic and environmental implications of the interaction between humans and machines.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Discuss broader implications of increasing interaction between humans and machines, including moral, ethical, social, economic and environmental aspects.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Raise awareness of the moral, ethical, social, economic and environmental implications of using science and technology.
coreConcepts: Human–machine interaction can change the nature of work and everyday life.
Moral and ethical questions include responsibility, autonomy and fairness.
There are economic and environmental consequences of widespread use of computing technologies.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming technological progress is always positive.
Ignoring long-term environmental costs of hardware production and disposal.
Believing that ethical issues can be solved purely by technical means.

conceptual: Discuss economic implications of increasing automation in manufacturing.
Discuss one ethical and one environmental implication of widespread use of smartphones.
examStyle: Discuss the moral, ethical, social, economic and environmental implications of the increased interaction between humans and machines in the workplace.
Evaluate the environmental implications of increased automation and human-machine interaction in modern manufacturing.

topics.title: Computer organization
topics.syllabusDescription: Structure and function of computer hardware, primary and secondary memory, operating systems, application software, data representation and simple logic.

subtopics.title: Outline architecture of the CPU and functions of ALU, CU and registers
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Outline the architecture of the central processing unit (CPU) and the functions of the arithmetic logic unit (ALU) and the control unit (CU) and the registers within the CPU.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Outline the basic architecture of the CPU and describe the functions of the ALU, control unit and registers such as MAR and MDR.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should be able to reproduce a block diagram showing the relationship between the elements of the CPU, input and output and storage. The memory address register (MAR) and memory data register (MDR) are the only registers that need to be included.
coreConcepts: The CPU executes instructions and coordinates activities of other components.
The ALU performs arithmetic and logical operations.
The control unit fetches and decodes instructions and controls execution.
Registers provide fast storage for addresses and data during processing.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing the roles of ALU and control unit.
Believing that all memory inside the CPU is the same as primary memory.
Ignoring the role of registers in instruction execution.

conceptual: Outline the function of the arithmetic logic unit (ALU).
Outline the role of the memory address register (MAR) in the CPU.
examStyle: Outline the architecture of the CPU, including the ALU, CU, registers, input/output and storage.
Describe the role of the control unit and the arithmetic logic unit during the execution of a program instruction.

subtopics.title: Describe primary memory
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Describe primary memory.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Describe primary memory and distinguish between random access memory (RAM) and read-only memory (ROM) and their uses.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Distinguish between random access memory (RAM) and read-only memory (ROM), and their use in primary memory.
coreConcepts: Primary memory stores data and instructions that are currently in use.
RAM is volatile memory that can be read and written during execution.
ROM is non-volatile memory used to store firmware such as the bootstrap program.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing RAM with secondary storage devices.
Believing that ROM can never be changed under any circumstances.
Using the term memory to refer only to secondary storage.

conceptual: Describe the difference between RAM and ROM.
Explain why RAM is described as volatile.
examStyle: Describe primary memory and distinguish between RAM and ROM.
Explain the difference between RAM and ROM and describe one use for each in a personal computer.

subtopics.title: Explain the use of cache memory
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Explain the use of cache memory.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Explain the role of cache memory in speeding up system performance and how it is used.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should be able to explain the effect of cache memory in speeding up the system as well as being able to explain how it is used.
coreConcepts: Cache memory is a small, fast memory that stores frequently accessed data and instructions.
Using cache reduces the average time to access data from main memory.
The effectiveness of cache relies on temporal and spatial locality.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing cache memory with virtual memory.
Assuming that increasing cache size always improves performance linearly.
Believing that cache stores all data permanently.

conceptual: Explain how cache memory can improve the performance of a computer system.
Explain why not all memory in a computer is implemented as cache.
examStyle: Explain the use of cache memory in a computer system.
Explain how the use of cache memory reduces the average time required for the CPU to access data.

subtopics.title: Explain the machine instruction cycle
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Explain the machine instruction cycle.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Explain the stages of the machine instruction cycle, including the role of the data bus and address bus.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: This should include the role of data bus and address bus.
coreConcepts: The machine instruction cycle typically consists of fetch, decode, execute and store stages.
The address bus carries addresses of instructions and data.
The data bus carries data and instructions between CPU and memory.
commonMisconceptions: Believing that all stages of the cycle are visible to the user.
Confusing the roles of data bus and address bus.
Ignoring the control signals required for the cycle.

conceptual: Explain the fetch–decode–execute cycle.
Explain the role of the address bus during the machine instruction cycle.
examStyle: Explain the machine instruction cycle, including the role of the data bus and address bus.
Describe the role of the data bus and address bus during the fetch stage of the machine instruction cycle.

subtopics.title: Identify the need for persistent storage
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Identify the need for persistent storage.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Identify why persistent storage is needed to store data in non-volatile devices during and after running programs.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Persistent storage is needed to store data in a non-volatile device during and after the running of a program.
coreConcepts: Persistent storage is required to keep data and programs when power is off.
Primary memory is volatile and cannot provide long-term storage.
Persistent storage is important for recovery after failures and for historical records.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming that saving to RAM is sufficient for persistence.
Believing that persistent storage never fails.
Ignoring the costs of storing and backing up large amounts of data.

conceptual: Identify two reasons why persistent storage is needed in a computer system.
Explain why persistent storage is necessary for an online banking system.
examStyle: Identify the need for persistent storage in a school information system.
Explain why persistent storage is essential in a mobile banking application even when the device is switched off.

subtopics.title: Describe main functions of an operating system
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Describe the main functions of an operating system.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Describe main functions of a single-user operating system, such as memory management, file management and user interface.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: This is confined to a single-user operating system. Technical details are not needed.
coreConcepts: The operating system manages hardware resources and provides services to applications.
Key functions include memory management, process management, file system management and user interface.
The OS provides an abstraction layer between hardware and application software.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing the operating system with application software.
Believing that users interact directly with hardware without the OS.
Assuming that all operating systems present the same interface and features.

conceptual: Describe two functions of an operating system.
Describe how an operating system manages files.
examStyle: Describe the main functions of a single-user operating system.
Explain the role of the operating system in managing processes and memory in a multi-tasking environment.

subtopics.title: Outline the use of a range of application software
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Outline the use of a range of application software.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Outline the use of application software such as word processors, spreadsheets, databases, email, web browsers, CAD and graphics software.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Application software should include word processors, spreadsheets, database management systems, email, web browsers, computer aided design (CAD) and graphic processing software.
coreConcepts: Application software helps users perform specific tasks.
Different applications are suited to different problem domains.
Some applications rely heavily on OS services and hardware capabilities.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming any application can be used for any type of task.
Confusing file formats with the applications that use them.
Believing that all application software has the same features.

conceptual: Outline one use of a spreadsheet in a business context.
Outline one use of a database management system in a school.
examStyle: Outline the use of three different types of application software in an organization.
Outline how a spreadsheet application and a database management system serve different purposes in a business context.

subtopics.title: Identify common features of applications
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Identify common features of applications.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Identify common user interface features of applications such as toolbars, menus, dialog boxes and GUI components.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Including toolbars, menus, dialogue boxes, graphical user interface (GUI) components. Some features are provided by the application software and some by the operating system.
coreConcepts: Many applications share common interface elements, which helps usability.
Some interface elements are provided by the OS and reused by applications.
Consistency across applications reduces the learning curve for users.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming that all interface elements are implemented separately by each application.
Believing that consistency between applications is accidental rather than designed.
Ignoring how the OS contributes to user interface components.

conceptual: Identify two common features of application software interfaces.
Identify one GUI component that is shared between many applications.
examStyle: Identify four common features found in many application software packages.
Explain how the cut, copy and paste feature found in many applications improves productivity for users.

subtopics.title: Define basic terms for binary representation
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Define the terms: bit, byte, binary, denary/decimal, hexadecimal.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Define bit, byte, binary, denary/decimal and hexadecimal.
coreConcepts: Bits are the basic unit of data in binary form.
Bytes are groups of bits, typically eight bits.
Binary, denary and hexadecimal are different number systems used in computing.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing decimal and binary representations of the same value.
Believing that hexadecimal is a different type of data rather than a notation.
Ignoring the relationship between bits and bytes.

conceptual: Define the term bit.
Define the term hexadecimal.
examStyle: Define the terms byte and binary.
Convert the denary number 156 to binary and to hexadecimal, showing your working.

subtopics.title: Outline how data is represented in the computer
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Outline the way in which data is represented in the computer.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Outline how data such as strings, integers, characters and colours are represented in binary form and consider storage space implications.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: To include strings, integers, characters and colours. This includes considering the space taken by data, for instance the relation between the hexadecimal representation of colours and the number of colours available.
coreConcepts: All data in a computer is ultimately represented as binary patterns.
Different data types use different encoding schemes and sizes.
Colour representation often uses hexadecimal notation to describe binary values.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming that text and numbers are stored in the same way.
Believing that character sets are the same across all languages.
Ignoring the storage cost of large data sets such as images or video.

conceptual: Outline how characters are represented in a computer system.
Outline how colours can be represented using hexadecimal values.
examStyle: Outline the way in which strings and colours are represented in a computer system.
Explain how a bitmap image is represented in binary in a computer system, referring to colour depth and resolution.

subtopics.title: Define Boolean operators
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Define the Boolean operators: AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR and XOR.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Define Boolean operators AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR and XOR.
coreConcepts: Boolean operators combine or invert truth values to produce logical results.
These operators form the basis of logical expressions and digital circuits.
Understanding these operators is essential for constructing truth tables and logic diagrams.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing NAND and NOR with AND and OR.
Assuming XOR behaves like OR for all inputs.
Ignoring that NOT inverts a single input value.

conceptual: Define the Boolean operator AND.
Define the Boolean operator XOR.
examStyle: Define the Boolean operators NOT and OR.
Construct the truth table for the Boolean expression A NAND B and describe what it means when both inputs are true.

subtopics.title: Construct truth tables using Boolean operators
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Construct truth tables using the above operators.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Construct truth tables for logical expressions using AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR and XOR, with up to three inputs.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Problems will be limited to an output dependent on no more than three inputs.
coreConcepts: Truth tables show the output of logical expressions for all possible input combinations.
They are essential for verifying the behaviour of logic circuits and conditions in programs.
Complex expressions can be broken down into intermediate columns in a truth table.
commonMisconceptions: Forgetting to include all input combinations.
Incorrectly applying operator precedence.
Confusing the outputs of similar operators such as OR and XOR.

conceptual: Construct a truth table for the expression A AND (NOT B).
Construct a truth table for the expression (A OR B) XOR C.
examStyle: Construct the truth table for the logical expression NOT(A AND B) OR C.
Construct the truth table for the expression (A OR B) AND (NOT C) for all possible input combinations.

subtopics.title: Construct a logic diagram using Boolean gates
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Construct a logic diagram using AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR and XOR gates.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Construct logic diagrams using AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR and XOR gates for expressions with up to three inputs.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Problems will be limited to an output dependent on no more than three inputs.
coreConcepts: Logic diagrams visually represent Boolean expressions using standard gate symbols.
Each gate corresponds to a Boolean operator with specific input–output behaviour.
Logic diagrams are used as blueprints for digital circuits.
commonMisconceptions: Misplacing inputs between gates and producing incorrect logic.
Using incorrect symbols for certain gates.
Forgetting to simplify expressions before drawing diagrams when appropriate.

conceptual: Construct a logic diagram for the expression A AND (B OR C).
Draw a logic diagram that outputs 1 only when exactly one of the two inputs is 1.
examStyle: Construct a logic diagram using AND, OR and NOT gates to represent the condition: Maria will go to school if it is not cold and it is not raining.
Construct a logic diagram using NAND gates only to represent the expression (A AND B) OR C.

topics.title: Networks
topics.syllabusDescription: Fundamentals of networking, data transmission, wireless networking and network security.

subtopics.title: Identify different types of networks
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Identify different types of networks.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Identify and describe different types of networks including LAN, VLAN, WAN, SAN, WLAN, internet, extranet, VPN, PAN and peer-to-peer.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Examples include local area network (LAN), virtual local area network (VLAN), wide area network (WAN), storage area network (SAN), wireless local area network (WLAN), internet, extranet, virtual private network (VPN), personal area network (PAN), peer-to-peer (P2P). Globalization has been accelerated by the technical advances linked to network development.
coreConcepts: Networks are classified by their geographic scope, topology and purpose.
A LAN covers a small area such as a building, while a WAN can span countries.
VPNs create secure private connections over public networks.
Peer-to-peer networks have no central server and each node acts as both client and server.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing WLAN with WAN because of similar names.
Assuming the internet and an intranet are the same.
Believing peer-to-peer networks are inherently less secure than client-server networks.

conceptual: Identify two differences between a LAN and a WAN.
Identify the type of network most suitable for connecting offices in two different countries.
examStyle: Identify four different types of networks and state one characteristic of each. [4]
Describe the difference between a LAN and a WAN and explain one scenario where each would be appropriate.

subtopics.title: Outline the importance of standards in the construction of networks
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Outline the importance of standards in the construction of networks.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Outline why standards are essential for compatibility and interoperability between network components and systems internationally.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Standards enable compatibility through a common language internationally.
coreConcepts: Standards ensure that devices from different manufacturers can communicate.
Without standards, networks would be fragmented and incompatible.
International standards bodies such as ISO and IEEE define and maintain network standards.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming standards are optional guidelines rather than requirements for interoperability.
Believing that standards limit innovation.
Ignoring the role of standards in international communication.

conceptual: Outline why standards are important when constructing a network that spans multiple countries.
Outline one consequence of not following network standards.
examStyle: Outline the importance of standards in the construction of networks. [4]
Explain why the lack of a universal standard can cause problems when building a network using hardware from different manufacturers.

subtopics.title: Describe how communication over networks is broken down into layers
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Describe how communication over networks is broken down into different layers.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Describe the concept of layered network models using the OSI seven-layer model as a reference.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Awareness of the OSI seven-layer model is required, but an understanding of the functioning of each layer is not.
coreConcepts: The OSI model breaks network communication into seven layers, each with a distinct role.
Layering allows each part of communication to be designed and maintained independently.
Each layer provides services to the layer above and uses services from the layer below.
commonMisconceptions: Memorizing every function of each OSI layer is not required at this level.
Believing the OSI model is the only layered networking model.
Assuming all networks strictly implement every OSI layer.

conceptual: Describe the purpose of breaking network communication into layers.
Describe what is meant by the OSI model.
examStyle: Describe how breaking network communication into layers can simplify network design and troubleshooting. [4]
Outline two advantages of using a layered protocol model when diagnosing faults in a network.

subtopics.title: Identify the technologies required to provide a VPN
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Identify the technologies required to provide a VPN.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Identify the key technologies used to create and maintain a VPN, including encryption, tunnelling protocols and authentication.
coreConcepts: A VPN uses encryption to secure data transmitted over a public network.
Tunnelling protocols encapsulate private network data within packets sent over a public network.
Authentication ensures that only authorized users can access the VPN.
commonMisconceptions: Believing a VPN makes all internet activity completely anonymous.
Assuming a VPN is only for remote workers.
Confusing a VPN with a proxy server.

conceptual: Identify two technologies required to provide a VPN.
Identify one protocol used in the creation of a VPN.
examStyle: Identify three technologies required to provide a VPN. [3]
Describe how encryption and authentication are used together to ensure security in a VPN connection.

subtopics.title: Evaluate the use of a VPN
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Evaluate the use of a VPN.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using a VPN, including security, remote access, cost and social implications.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: The use of a VPN has led to changes in working patterns.
coreConcepts: VPNs provide secure remote access to organizational resources.
VPN use has enabled flexible and remote working patterns.
Potential drawbacks include reduced connection speed and ongoing infrastructure cost.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming VPNs guarantee total privacy without limitations.
Believing VPNs eliminate the need for other security measures.
Ignoring the performance overhead introduced by encryption.

conceptual: Evaluate the use of a VPN for employees working from home.
Discuss one social implication of widespread VPN use in the workplace.
examStyle: Evaluate the use of a VPN for a company with employees working in multiple countries. [8]
Discuss two disadvantages of using a VPN that an organization should consider before implementation.

subtopics.title: Define the terms: protocol, data packet
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Define the terms: protocol, data packet.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Define protocol and data packet in the context of network communication.
coreConcepts: A protocol is a set of rules governing how data is transmitted between devices.
A data packet is a unit of data transmitted over a network, containing header and payload.
Protocols ensure that communication is structured and understood by both sender and receiver.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing protocols with physical network hardware.
Believing data packets always arrive in order.
Assuming all packets in a transmission are the same size.

conceptual: Define the term protocol.
Define the term data packet.
examStyle: Define the terms protocol and data packet. [2]
Explain how data packets use protocol information to ensure correct delivery across a network.

subtopics.title: Explain why protocols are necessary
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Explain why protocols are necessary.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Explain the necessity of protocols in network communication, including data integrity, flow control, deadlock, congestion and error checking.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Including data integrity, flow control, deadlock, congestion, error checking.
coreConcepts: Protocols ensure data is transmitted reliably and interpreted correctly.
Flow control prevents a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver.
Error checking detects and sometimes corrects data corruption during transmission.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming data always arrives intact without error checking.
Believing flow control is only needed on slow networks.
Thinking deadlock and congestion are the same problem.

conceptual: Explain why error checking is a necessary part of network protocols.
Explain how flow control helps prevent data loss in network communication.
examStyle: Explain why protocols are necessary in network communication. [6]
Describe what would happen if two devices on the same network used different communication protocols.

subtopics.title: Explain why the speed of data transmission across a network can vary
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Explain why the speed of data transmission across a network can vary.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Explain factors that affect data transmission speed, including bandwidth, latency, congestion, transmission medium and network protocols.
coreConcepts: Bandwidth is the maximum capacity of a transmission medium.
Latency is the delay in sending data from source to destination.
Network congestion and interference can significantly reduce effective data transfer rates.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing bandwidth with actual throughput.
Assuming wired connections are always faster than wireless.
Ignoring the effect of protocol overhead on effective speed.

conceptual: Explain two reasons why the speed of data transmission across a network can vary.
Explain the difference between bandwidth and throughput.
examStyle: Explain three factors that can cause the speed of data transmission across a network to vary. [6]
Outline two factors that can reduce data transmission speed in a heavily used corporate network.

subtopics.title: Explain why compression of data is often necessary when transmitting across a network
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Explain why compression of data is often necessary when transmitting across a network.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Explain the role and need for data compression in network transmission, including bandwidth limitations and transmission time.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Compression has enabled information to be disseminated more rapidly.
coreConcepts: Data compression reduces file sizes, allowing faster transmission over limited bandwidth.
Lossless compression preserves all original data, while lossy compression discards some data.
Compression enables multimedia content to be distributed rapidly over the internet.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming all compression is lossless.
Believing compression always results in quality loss.
Ignoring the processing overhead required to compress and decompress data.

conceptual: Explain why compression is necessary when streaming video over the internet.
Explain the difference between lossy and lossless compression.
examStyle: Explain why data compression is often necessary when transmitting multimedia files across a network. [6]
Compare lossy and lossless compression and explain which would be more appropriate for transmitting medical scan images.

subtopics.title: Outline the characteristics of different transmission media
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Outline the characteristics of different transmission media.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Outline the characteristics of metal conductor, fibre optic and wireless transmission media, including speed, reliability, cost and security.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Characteristics include speed, reliability, cost and security. Transmission media include metal conductor, fibre optic, wireless.
coreConcepts: Metal conductors are widely used but susceptible to electromagnetic interference and have limited bandwidth.
Fibre optic cables offer high speed and are immune to electromagnetic interference, but are more expensive.
Wireless media offers flexibility and mobility but is more vulnerable to security threats and interference.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming wireless is always slower than wired media.
Believing fibre optic cables are fragile and impractical.
Ignoring security vulnerabilities of wireless transmission.

conceptual: Outline one advantage and one disadvantage of using fibre optic cable over metal conductor.
Outline two characteristics of wireless transmission media.
examStyle: Outline the characteristics of metal conductor, fibre optic and wireless transmission media in terms of speed, cost and security. [6]
Compare fibre optic and wireless transmission media in terms of speed, cost, and security.

subtopics.title: Explain how data is transmitted by packet switching
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Explain how data is transmitted by packet switching.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Explain the concept of packet switching including how data is split into packets, routed independently and reassembled at the destination.
coreConcepts: In packet switching, data is split into small packets that are sent independently across a network.
Each packet contains a header with addressing and sequencing information.
Packets may take different routes and are reassembled in the correct order at the destination.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming all packets in a message follow the same path.
Believing packet switching is only used for large files.
Confusing packet switching with circuit switching.

conceptual: Explain how a large file is transmitted using packet switching.
Explain why packets from the same message may arrive out of order.
examStyle: Explain how data is transmitted across the internet using packet switching. [6]
Explain how packet switching allows multiple users to share the same network infrastructure simultaneously.

subtopics.title: Outline the advantages and disadvantages of wireless networks
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Outline the advantages and disadvantages of wireless networks.
