subtopics.syllabusContent: Outline the advantages and disadvantages of wireless networks, including mobility, cost, security risks and health concerns.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Wireless networks have led to changes in working patterns, social activities and raised health issues.
coreConcepts: Wireless networks provide mobility and ease of setup without physical cables.
Security risks are greater with wireless networks as signals can be intercepted.
Wireless networks have changed working and social patterns significantly.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming wireless networks are always less reliable.
Believing that WPA2 encryption makes wireless networks completely secure.
Ignoring potential health concerns associated with wireless radiation.

conceptual: Outline two advantages and two disadvantages of using a wireless network in a school.
Outline one social implication of widespread wireless network use.
examStyle: Outline the advantages and disadvantages of wireless networks in a hospital environment. [6]
Evaluate the suitability of a wireless network for use in a large public library serving hundreds of simultaneous users.

subtopics.title: Describe the hardware and software components of a wireless network
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Describe the hardware and software components of a wireless network.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Describe hardware components such as wireless access points, routers and network interface cards, and software components such as network drivers and security software.
coreConcepts: Wireless networks require access points to broadcast the network signal.
Network interface cards (NICs) in client devices allow them to connect wirelessly.
Software components include drivers, firmware and security protocols to manage connections.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming a router and a wireless access point are always the same device.
Ignoring the software components required to configure and secure a wireless network.
Believing that any device can connect to any wireless network without configuration.

conceptual: Describe two hardware components required for a wireless network.
Describe one software component required to manage a wireless network.
examStyle: Describe the hardware and software components required to set up a wireless network in an office. [6]
Explain the role of a wireless access point and a network interface card in establishing a wireless connection.

subtopics.title: Describe the characteristics of wireless networks
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Describe the characteristics of wireless networks.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Describe the characteristics of wireless network technologies including WiFi, WiMAX, 3G mobile and future networks.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Include WiFi, Worldwide Interoperability for Microwave Access (WiMAX), 3G mobile and future networks. Connectivity between different locations.
coreConcepts: WiFi is designed for short-range local area wireless networking.
WiMAX provides longer-range wireless broadband connectivity.
3G and successive mobile standards enable internet access via cellular networks.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming WiFi and WiMAX serve the same purpose.
Believing 3G and WiFi are interchangeable technologies.
Thinking future wireless standards will not introduce new capabilities or limitations.

conceptual: Describe two characteristics that distinguish WiFi from WiMAX.
Describe one advantage of 3G mobile networks over WiFi.
examStyle: Describe the characteristics of WiFi and WiMAX as wireless network technologies. [6]
Compare WiFi and Bluetooth as wireless communication technologies in terms of range and typical application.

subtopics.title: Describe the different methods of network security
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Describe the different methods of network security.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Describe network security methods including encryption, user IDs and passwords, and trusted MAC addresses.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Include encryption types, userID, trusted media access control (MAC) addresses. Wireless networks have led to concerns about the security of the user's data.
coreConcepts: Encryption scrambles data so that only authorized parties can read it.
User IDs and passwords restrict access to authorized users.
MAC address filtering allows only recognized devices to connect to a network.
commonMisconceptions: Believing WEP encryption is still a secure option.
Assuming a password alone is sufficient network security.
Thinking MAC address filtering cannot be bypassed.

conceptual: Describe how encryption can be used to protect data on a wireless network.
Describe how MAC address filtering works as a security measure.
examStyle: Describe three methods that can be used to improve the security of a wireless network. [6]
Outline two methods that can be used to prevent unauthorized users from accessing a wireless network.

subtopics.title: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of each method of network security
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of each method of network security.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of different network security methods in various contexts.
coreConcepts: No single security method is completely foolproof and each has limitations.
Strong encryption may introduce performance overhead.
Layering multiple security methods provides stronger overall protection.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming the most complex security method is always the best choice.
Believing security measures do not affect usability or performance.
Ignoring insider threats when evaluating network security.

conceptual: Evaluate the use of WPA2 encryption as the sole security method for a public WiFi hotspot.
Evaluate MAC address filtering as a method of securing a school wireless network.
examStyle: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using encryption and MAC address filtering to secure a wireless network. [8]
Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using a firewall and intrusion detection system together to secure a corporate network.

topics.title: General principles of computational thinking
topics.syllabusDescription: Thinking procedurally, logically, ahead, concurrently and abstractly as applied to problem solving.

subtopics.title: Identify the procedure appropriate to solving a problem
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Identify the procedure appropriate to solving a problem.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Identify the steps needed to solve a problem and place them in the correct order.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: This includes identifying the steps and putting them in the correct order. Such as recipes, block-arrow-block-arrow.
coreConcepts: Procedural thinking involves breaking a task into an ordered sequence of steps.
Steps must be ordered correctly or the desired outcome will not be achieved.
Real-world analogies such as recipes illustrate procedural thinking.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming any order of steps will produce the same result.
Confusing a procedure with a random list of actions.
Ignoring edge cases when defining a procedure.

conceptual: Identify the steps to find the largest value in a list of numbers.
Identify the correct order of steps to log in to a website securely.
examStyle: Identify the steps required to sort a list of names into alphabetical order. [4]
Describe how decomposing a complex problem into smaller subproblems makes it easier to develop and test a solution.

subtopics.title: Evaluate whether the order of activities will result in the required outcome
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Evaluate whether the order in which activities are undertaken will result in the required outcome.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Evaluate whether a given sequence of steps will correctly achieve the intended outcome.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Links to problems presented to the student in other areas of the syllabus.
coreConcepts: The order of steps in a procedure directly determines whether the correct result is produced.
Incorrect ordering can produce wrong results or cause errors.
Evaluating order requires tracing through each step and assessing its effect.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming that a procedure that looks reasonable will always produce the correct result.
Ignoring the effect of prior steps on later ones.

conceptual: Evaluate whether the following sequence of steps for boiling water is in the correct order.
Evaluate whether a given algorithm correctly sorts an array.
examStyle: Evaluate whether the given sequence of steps will result in a list being sorted in ascending order. [6]
Construct a trace table to show the values of variables as a loop calculates the sum of integers from 1 to 5.

subtopics.title: Explain the role of sub-procedures in solving a problem
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Explain the role of sub-procedures in solving a problem.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Explain how breaking a problem into sub-procedures that can be called by name supports modularity and reuse.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Constructing procedures that can then be referred to by their identifier.
coreConcepts: Sub-procedures allow complex problems to be broken into smaller, manageable parts.
Once defined, a sub-procedure can be called by name from multiple places.
Using sub-procedures improves readability, reuse and ease of debugging.
commonMisconceptions: Believing sub-procedures are only useful in large programs.
Assuming sub-procedures always need to return a value.
Confusing sub-procedures with data structures.

conceptual: Explain why using sub-procedures improves the maintainability of a large program.
Explain how a sub-procedure for validating input could be reused in multiple parts of a system.
examStyle: Explain the role of sub-procedures in solving a complex problem. [6]
Explain the difference between a pre-condition loop and a post-condition loop and give one situation where a post-condition loop would be preferred.

subtopics.title: Identify when decision-making is required in a specified situation
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Identify when decision-making is required in a specified situation.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Identify points in a problem or process where a decision must be made based on a condition.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Links to procedural thinking and alternative procedures.
coreConcepts: Decision-making occurs when different actions must be taken depending on the state of the system.
Decisions are represented in algorithms using conditional constructs such as IF-THEN-ELSE.
Identifying decision points is a key step in designing correct algorithms.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming a procedure with no decisions is always simpler or better.
Confusing sequential steps with decision points.
Ignoring the case where neither branch of a decision applies.

conceptual: Identify the point in a password checking algorithm where a decision is required.
Identify two decision points in the process of issuing a library book.
examStyle: Identify two situations within a ticket booking system that require decision-making. [4]
Explain how selection statements allow a program to respond differently depending on the value of a variable.

subtopics.title: Identify the decisions required for the solution to a specified problem
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Identify the decisions required for the solution to a specified problem.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Identify all decisions and the conditions on which they depend in a given problem.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Different actions are taken based on conditions.
coreConcepts: A solution may require multiple decisions, each dependent on different conditions.
Listing all required decisions ensures that the algorithm handles all possible cases.
Missing a required decision can lead to incorrect or incomplete solutions.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming a single decision covers all cases.
Forgetting to consider what happens when a condition is false.
Confusing a decision with a loop.

conceptual: Identify all the decisions required to calculate the end-of-year grade for a student.
Identify the decisions needed to validate a user login attempt.
examStyle: Identify three decisions required to solve the problem of finding the second largest value in a list. [3]
Construct pseudocode for an algorithm that reads 10 exam scores into an array and outputs the highest score.

subtopics.title: Identify the condition associated with a given decision in a specified problem
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Identify the condition associated with a given decision in a specified problem.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Identify Boolean conditions using AND, OR and NOT relationships for decisions in a problem.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Testing conditions, iteration. Identifying and constructing the conditions using AND, OR, NOT relationships and Boolean tests.
coreConcepts: Every decision in an algorithm is based on a condition that evaluates to true or false.
Conditions can be compound, combining multiple sub-conditions with AND, OR or NOT.
Identifying the precise condition for each decision is essential for correct algorithm design.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming a condition can have more than two outcomes without additional logic.
Mixing up AND and OR in compound conditions.
Forgetting that NOT reverses the truth value of a condition.

conceptual: Identify the condition required to check if a number is both positive and even.
Identify the condition associated with deciding whether a user is eligible for a discount.
examStyle: Identify the Boolean condition required at each decision point in a given algorithm. [4]
Explain the difference between passing a parameter by value and passing a parameter by reference, giving one example of each.

subtopics.title: Explain the relationship between the decisions and conditions of a system
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Explain the relationship between the decisions and conditions of a system.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Explain how IF-THEN-ELSE constructs link conditions to actions in an algorithm.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: IF ... THEN ... ELSE.
coreConcepts: An IF-THEN-ELSE construct executes one block of code if a condition is true and another if it is false.
The condition determines which branch is taken.
Nested conditions allow complex decision trees to be represented.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing the THEN and ELSE branches.
Believing every IF must have an ELSE.
Assuming that nested IF statements always produce the same result as compound conditions.

conceptual: Explain how an IF-THEN-ELSE construct links a condition to alternative actions.
Explain the difference between a simple IF statement and an IF-THEN-ELSE statement.
examStyle: Explain the relationship between decisions and conditions in an algorithm that classifies student grades. [6]
Describe two advantages of using subroutines when developing a large software system.

subtopics.title: Deduce logical rules for real-world situations
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Deduce logical rules for real-world situations.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Deduce appropriate Boolean logical rules from real-world problem descriptions.
coreConcepts: Real-world decision situations can be expressed as logical rules using Boolean operators.
Deducing logical rules requires careful interpretation of problem requirements.
Logical rules form the basis of conditional statements in algorithms.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming English descriptions of conditions translate directly and simply to Boolean logic.
Ignoring edge cases in logical rules.
Confusing inclusive OR with exclusive OR in everyday language.

conceptual: Deduce the logical rule for a door that opens only when a card is valid AND a PIN is correct.
Deduce the logical rule for a student who passes if they pass the exam OR complete all coursework.
examStyle: Deduce the logical rule for admitting a visitor who has a valid ticket and is over 18, or who is accompanied by an adult. [4]
Explain how a recursive function uses a call stack and describe what happens if the base case is never reached.

subtopics.title: Identify the inputs and outputs required in a solution
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Identify the inputs and outputs required in a solution.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Identify what data a solution requires as input and what it should produce as output.
coreConcepts: Every algorithmic solution has defined inputs and expected outputs.
Clearly identifying inputs and outputs is a prerequisite for designing a correct algorithm.
The same problem may have different inputs and outputs depending on context.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing intermediate variables with inputs or outputs.
Assuming all outputs are displayed to users.
Forgetting that some algorithms may have no explicit inputs.

conceptual: Identify the inputs and outputs for an algorithm that calculates a student's average grade.
Identify the outputs required from a hotel booking system.
examStyle: Identify the inputs and outputs required for an algorithm that finds the maximum value in an array. [4]
Construct pseudocode for a binary search algorithm that searches a sorted array of integers for a given target value.

subtopics.title: Identify pre-planning in a suggested problem and solution
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Identify pre-planning in a suggested problem and solution.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Identify examples of pre-planning such as pre-ordering, caching, Gantt charts and building reusable libraries.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Gantt charts. Pre-ordering. Pre-heating an oven. Home/locker/knapsack. Caching/pre-fetching. Building libraries of pre-formed elements for future use.
coreConcepts: Pre-planning involves preparing resources or data in advance to improve efficiency.
Caching stores frequently accessed data close to where it is needed.
Pre-ordering data structures reduces the cost of later operations.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming pre-planning is always worthwhile regardless of context.
Confusing pre-planning with over-engineering.
Ignoring the cost of pre-planning when resources are limited.

conceptual: Identify one example of pre-planning in a restaurant kitchen.
Identify how caching is an example of thinking ahead in a computer system.
examStyle: Identify two examples of pre-planning in the context of organizing a school sports day. [4]
Compare the efficiency of a binary search and a sequential search for locating a record in a sorted list of 1000 items.

subtopics.title: Explain the need for pre-conditions when executing an algorithm
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Explain the need for pre-conditions when executing an algorithm.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Explain why certain conditions must be satisfied before an algorithm can execute correctly.
coreConcepts: Pre-conditions define what must be true about inputs or state before an algorithm starts.
Violating pre-conditions can lead to incorrect results or runtime errors.
Documenting pre-conditions improves algorithm clarity and correctness.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming an algorithm handles all possible inputs without restriction.
Confusing pre-conditions with post-conditions.
Ignoring pre-conditions when testing algorithms.

conceptual: Explain why a binary search algorithm requires the list to be sorted as a pre-condition.
Explain one pre-condition required before executing a division algorithm.
examStyle: Explain why pre-conditions are necessary when executing an algorithm that calculates an employee's weekly wage. [6]
Explain how a selection sort algorithm works and construct a trace showing how the list [4, 2, 7, 1] is sorted.

subtopics.title: Outline the pre- and post-conditions to a specified problem
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Outline the pre- and post-conditions to a specified problem.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Outline the pre-conditions (what must be true before) and post-conditions (what must be true after) for a given algorithm.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: For example, cooking a dish for a meal. All ingredients available before starting to cook. A place to eat the food.
coreConcepts: Pre-conditions describe the required state before an algorithm begins.
Post-conditions describe the guaranteed state after an algorithm completes.
Together they form a contract specifying how the algorithm should behave.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing pre-conditions with the algorithm steps themselves.
Assuming post-conditions are automatically verified.
Ignoring the case where pre-conditions are not met.

conceptual: Outline the pre- and post-conditions for an algorithm that removes duplicate values from an array.
Outline the pre-conditions for a login algorithm.
examStyle: Outline the pre- and post-conditions for an algorithm that sorts a list of student names. [4]
Construct pseudocode to declare and populate a two-dimensional array representing the seats in a 5-row, 8-column cinema.

subtopics.title: Identify exceptions that need to be considered in a specified problem solution
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Identify exceptions that need to be considered in a specified problem solution.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Identify edge cases, exceptions and boundary conditions that may affect the correctness of a solution.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: For example, identify the pre-conditions for calculating the end-of-year bonus when not all employees have worked for the company for the whole year.
coreConcepts: Exceptions are situations that fall outside the normal expected flow of an algorithm.
Failing to handle exceptions can cause algorithms to produce incorrect results or crash.
Identifying exceptions early in design prevents problems during implementation.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming the main path of an algorithm handles all cases.
Confusing exceptions with syntax errors.
Ignoring input validation as a source of exceptions.

conceptual: Identify two exceptions that must be considered in an algorithm calculating an employee bonus.
Identify the exceptions that could arise when dividing two numbers input by a user.
examStyle: Identify three exceptions that need to be considered in a solution for processing online orders. [3]
Explain how a collection differs from an array and describe one operation that is possible with a collection but not a standard array.

subtopics.title: Identify the parts of a solution that could be implemented concurrently
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Identify the parts of a solution that could be implemented concurrently.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Identify independent tasks within a solution that can be performed at the same time.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Could include computer systems or real-life situations.
coreConcepts: Concurrent processing involves performing multiple tasks at the same time.
Tasks can be run concurrently only if they are independent of each other.
Identifying concurrent tasks can significantly reduce total completion time.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming all tasks can be run concurrently.
Confusing concurrency with simply doing things faster.
Ignoring dependencies between tasks that prevent concurrent execution.

conceptual: Identify two parts of a house construction process that could be carried out concurrently.
Identify which steps of a data processing pipeline could run at the same time.
examStyle: Identify two tasks in the process of preparing a meal that could be carried out concurrently. [2]
Describe how abstract data types allow a programmer to use a data structure without needing to know its internal implementation.

subtopics.title: Describe how concurrent processing can be used to solve a problem
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Describe how concurrent processing can be used to solve a problem.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Describe how dividing a problem into concurrent tasks can improve efficiency, using examples such as production lines and division of labour.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: For example, building a house, production lines, division of labour. Students will not be expected to construct a flow chart or pseudocode related to concurrent processing.
coreConcepts: Concurrent processing can reduce the overall time needed to complete a task.
Real-world analogies such as production lines illustrate the principle of concurrency.
Concurrent tasks must not interfere with each other to produce correct results.
commonMisconceptions: Believing concurrent processing always requires specialized hardware.
Assuming concurrent tasks will always finish at the same time.
Ignoring synchronization problems that can arise in concurrent systems.

conceptual: Describe how concurrent processing is used in a car assembly production line.
Describe how dividing work between team members illustrates concurrent processing.
examStyle: Describe how concurrent processing could be used to speed up the rendering of frames in a video. [6]
Describe how a stack data structure operates and explain one application where a stack is used in a compiler.

subtopics.title: Evaluate the decision to use concurrent processing in solving a problem
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Evaluate the decision to use concurrent processing in solving a problem.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Evaluate the benefits and drawbacks of using concurrent processing for a given problem.
coreConcepts: Concurrent processing can improve performance but introduces complexity and potential synchronization issues.
Not all problems benefit from concurrent processing.
The decision to use concurrency must weigh potential gains against added complexity.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming concurrent processing always improves performance.
Ignoring the overhead of managing concurrent tasks.
Believing concurrency eliminates the need for sequential logic.

conceptual: Evaluate whether concurrent processing would benefit a sequential data validation process.
Evaluate one advantage and one disadvantage of using concurrent processing in an online search engine.
examStyle: Evaluate the decision to use concurrent processing when processing a large dataset of student exam results. [8]
Explain how a queue data structure operates and describe one real-world application of a queue in an operating system.

subtopics.title: Identify examples of abstraction
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Identify examples of abstraction.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Identify examples where irrelevant details are removed to focus on what matters for solving a problem.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Selecting the pieces of information that are relevant to solving the problem.
coreConcepts: Abstraction involves filtering out unnecessary detail to focus on what is relevant.
It is used in designing algorithms, data structures and systems.
Everyday examples include maps, diagrams and schedules.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking abstraction means removing all detail.
Confusing abstraction with approximation.
Assuming abstraction always makes a problem easier to solve.

conceptual: Identify two examples of abstraction used in everyday life.
Identify what information a map abstracts from the real world.
examStyle: Identify two examples of abstraction in the design of a school management system. [4]
Explain how a linked list allows efficient insertion and deletion of elements compared to an array.

subtopics.title: Explain why abstraction is required in the derivation of computational solutions
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Explain why abstraction is required in the derivation of computational solutions for a specified situation.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Explain why removing unnecessary details allows computational solutions to be designed and implemented efficiently.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should be aware of the concept of objects, for example, the use of collections as objects in the design of algorithms.
coreConcepts: Abstraction reduces complexity by hiding irrelevant implementation details.
It enables the development of reusable and maintainable solutions.
Objects and collections are examples of abstraction in computational thinking.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming abstraction is only relevant to object-oriented programming.
Believing abstraction makes solutions less accurate.
Ignoring the importance of choosing the right level of abstraction.

conceptual: Explain why abstraction is needed when designing a computational model of a city's traffic system.
Explain how using a collection object abstracts the management of multiple data items.
examStyle: Explain why abstraction is required when developing a computer simulation of a hospital ward. [6]
Construct a diagram showing the state of a binary search tree after inserting the values 8, 3, 10, 1, 6 in that order.

subtopics.title: Construct an abstraction from a specified situation
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Construct an abstraction from a specified situation.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Construct an abstraction by identifying relevant information and decomposing a situation into meaningful levels.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: There is no need to use code. Levels of abstraction through successive decomposition. A school can be decomposed into faculties; a faculty into departments.
coreConcepts: Successive decomposition breaks a system down into increasingly specific levels.
Each level of abstraction hides the complexity of the levels below it.
Constructing an abstraction requires selecting what is relevant at each level.
commonMisconceptions: Including too much or too little detail at each level of abstraction.
Confusing decomposition with simply listing features.
Assuming abstraction must be expressed in code.

conceptual: Construct an abstraction of a university by decomposing it into faculties and departments.
Construct an abstraction of a library system, identifying the relevant entities and ignoring irrelevant details.
examStyle: Construct an abstraction of a hospital by decomposing it into appropriate levels. [6]
Explain the difference between a static and a dynamic data structure and describe one advantage of each.

subtopics.title: Distinguish between a real-world entity and its abstraction
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Distinguish between a real-world entity and its abstraction.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Distinguish between actual real-world objects or systems and the simplified models or representations used in computing.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: The map as an abstraction of the territory.
coreConcepts: An abstraction is a simplified model that captures only the relevant properties of a real-world entity.
A map is an abstraction of physical territory; a class is an abstraction of a real-world object.
The abstraction is not the same as the entity it represents.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming that an abstraction is always a complete and accurate representation.
Confusing the abstraction with the thing being modelled.
Believing that a better abstraction contains more detail.

conceptual: Distinguish between a real person and a student record in a database.
Distinguish between a physical road network and a GPS route map.
examStyle: Distinguish between a real-world school and its abstraction in a school management system. [4]
Describe how a hash table uses a hash function to store data and explain what is meant by a collision.

topics.title: Connecting computational thinking and program design
topics.syllabusDescription: Standard algorithms, algorithm analysis, pseudocode and flow chart interpretation and construction.

subtopics.title: Describe the characteristics of standard algorithms on linear arrays
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Describe the characteristics of standard algorithms on linear arrays.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Describe the characteristics of sequential search, binary search, bubble sort and selection sort.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: These are: sequential search, binary search, bubble sort, selection sort.
coreConcepts: Sequential search checks each element in order until the target is found.
Binary search requires a sorted array and repeatedly halves the search space.
Bubble sort compares adjacent elements and swaps them if out of order.
Selection sort finds the minimum element and places it in the correct position.
commonMisconceptions: Applying binary search to unsorted arrays.
Assuming bubble sort is efficient for large datasets.
Confusing selection sort with insertion sort.

conceptual: Describe how a binary search works on a sorted array of integers.
Describe the steps of a bubble sort algorithm on a small array.
examStyle: Describe the characteristics of sequential search and binary search, and state one advantage of binary search. [6]
Describe the characteristics of a bubble sort algorithm on a linear array and state one scenario where it is inefficient.

subtopics.title: Outline the standard operations of collections
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Outline the standard operations of collections.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Outline the standard operations of collections including addition and retrieval of data.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: These are: addition and retrieval of data.
coreConcepts: Collections store groups of related data items.
The two fundamental operations are adding data to the collection and retrieving data from it.
Collections abstract the management of multiple items under a single identifier.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing collections with arrays.
Assuming retrieval always returns items in the order they were added.
Believing all collections support the same set of operations.

conceptual: Outline the two standard operations of a collection.
Outline how the add operation of a collection differs from assignment to an array element.
examStyle: Outline the standard operations that can be performed on a collection. [4]
Describe how the hasnext() and getnext() operations of a collection are used together to iterate through all its elements.

subtopics.title: Discuss an algorithm to solve a specific problem
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Discuss an algorithm to solve a specific problem.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Discuss the suitability, advantages and disadvantages of algorithms for solving a given problem, including standard and novel algorithms.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should be expected to discuss the differences between algorithms, including both standard and novel algorithms. For example, discussing the advantages and disadvantages of using a binary search as opposed to a sequential search.
coreConcepts: Different algorithms can solve the same problem with different efficiency and constraints.
Choosing an algorithm requires evaluating its correctness, efficiency and applicability.
Binary search is more efficient than sequential search but requires sorted data.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming the fastest algorithm is always the best choice.
Ignoring constraints such as whether data is sorted.
Believing there is always one best algorithm for every problem.

conceptual: Discuss whether binary search or sequential search is more appropriate for searching an unsorted list.
Discuss the suitability of bubble sort for sorting a nearly sorted list.
examStyle: Discuss the relative advantages and disadvantages of using bubble sort versus selection sort on a list of 1000 integers. [8]
Discuss the relative advantages of using a binary search compared to a sequential search for locating a record in a sorted list of 10 000 items.

subtopics.title: Analyse an algorithm presented as a flow chart
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Analyse an algorithm presented as a flow chart.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Analyse flow charts including tracing execution, assessing correctness, and understanding variables, calculations, loops and conditionals.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Examination questions may involve variables, calculations, simple and nested loops, simple conditionals and multiple or nested conditionals. This would include tracing an algorithm as well as assessing its correctness. Students will not be expected to construct a flow chart in an externally assessed component.
coreConcepts: Tracing a flow chart means following the execution path step by step for given inputs.
Flow charts can contain simple and nested loops and conditional branches.
Analysing a flow chart includes verifying whether it correctly solves its intended problem.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing the direction of flow chart arrows.
Skipping loop iterations when tracing.
Assuming a flow chart that looks correct always produces the right output.

conceptual: Trace the flow chart for a bubble sort algorithm with the input [5, 3, 1, 4, 2].
Identify an error in the given flow chart for finding the maximum value in an array.
examStyle: Analyse the following flow chart and state the output for the given input values. [8]
Analyse the following flow chart that calculates the factorial of a number and determine the output when the input is 4.

subtopics.title: Analyse an algorithm presented as pseudocode
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Analyse an algorithm presented as pseudocode.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Analyse pseudocode algorithms including tracing execution, assessing correctness and understanding variables, loops and conditionals.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Examination questions may involve variables, calculations, simple and nested loops, simple conditionals and multiple or nested conditionals. This would include tracing an algorithm as well as assessing its correctness.
coreConcepts: Tracing pseudocode involves following each instruction in order and recording variable values.
Pseudocode uses a structured but informal language to describe algorithm logic.
Analysing pseudocode includes identifying the purpose, correctness and efficiency of an algorithm.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing pseudocode syntax with a specific programming language.
Forgetting to update loop variables when tracing.
Assuming pseudocode is always correct if it looks syntactically valid.

conceptual: Trace the following pseudocode and state the output for input values X = 5 and Y = 3.
Identify a logic error in the given pseudocode for computing a factorial.
examStyle: Analyse the following pseudocode algorithm and state the value of each variable after each iteration of the loop. [8]
Analyse the following pseudocode algorithm and identify any logic errors, explaining how each would affect the output.

subtopics.title: Construct pseudocode to represent an algorithm
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Construct pseudocode to represent an algorithm.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Construct pseudocode using standard constructs including loops, conditionals, variables and sub-procedures.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Teachers must ensure students use the approved notation sheet.
coreConcepts: Pseudocode expresses algorithm logic clearly without being tied to a specific programming language.
Students must follow the approved IB pseudocode notation.
Well-written pseudocode can be directly translated into working code.
commonMisconceptions: Using programming language-specific syntax instead of approved pseudocode notation.
Writing pseudocode that is too vague to be implemented.
Confusing pseudocode with a natural language description of steps.

conceptual: Construct pseudocode for an algorithm that finds the sum of all even numbers in an array.
Construct pseudocode for a binary search on a sorted array.
examStyle: Construct pseudocode for an algorithm that reads 10 numbers from the user and outputs the largest. [8]
Construct pseudocode for an algorithm that reads a list of student names and scores and outputs the name of the student with the highest score.

subtopics.title: Suggest suitable algorithms to solve a specific problem
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Suggest suitable algorithms to solve a specific problem.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Suggest algorithms that correctly solve a problem, considering efficiency, correctness, reliability and flexibility.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Suitable algorithms may include both standard algorithms and novel algorithms. Suitable may include considerations of efficiency, correctness, reliability and flexibility. Students are expected to suggest algorithms that will actually solve the problem successfully.
coreConcepts: A suitable algorithm must correctly solve the problem within the given constraints.
Efficiency, reliability and flexibility are factors in choosing an appropriate algorithm.
Novel algorithms may be needed when standard algorithms do not fit the problem.
commonMisconceptions: Suggesting an efficient algorithm that does not actually solve the problem.
Ignoring constraints such as sorted input requirements.
Assuming the most well-known algorithm is always most suitable.

conceptual: Suggest a suitable algorithm for finding a specific student record in a sorted database.
Suggest a suitable sorting algorithm for a list that is already nearly sorted.
examStyle: Suggest a suitable algorithm for searching a sorted array of 10 000 names and justify your choice. [6]
Suggest a suitable sorting algorithm for arranging a small list of 8 names alphabetically and justify your answer.

subtopics.title: Deduce the efficiency of an algorithm in the context of its use
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Deduce the efficiency of an algorithm in the context of its use.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Deduce the relative efficiency of algorithms by analysing their loop structures and suggesting improvements.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should understand and explain the difference in efficiency between a single loop, nested loops, a loop that ends when a condition is met or questions of similar complexity. Students should also be able to suggest changes that would improve efficiency, for example, using a flag to stop a search immediately when an item is found.
coreConcepts: A single loop iterates linearly; nested loops iterate quadratically for most inputs.
Early termination using a flag can significantly reduce the number of iterations.
Algorithm efficiency depends on both the algorithm structure and the input data.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming nested loops always run n squared times.
Ignoring best-case performance when evaluating algorithms.
Confusing code readability with efficiency.

conceptual: Deduce which of two given algorithms is more efficient and explain why.
Suggest how adding a flag variable to a search algorithm could improve its efficiency.
examStyle: Deduce the efficiency of the following pseudocode algorithm and suggest one improvement. [6]
Deduce whether a sequential search or a binary search would be more efficient for searching an unsorted list of 500 elements, justifying your answer.

subtopics.title: Determine the number of times a step in an algorithm will be performed for given input data
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Determine the number of times a step in an algorithm will be performed for given input data.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Determine the exact or range of number of times a specific step executes for given inputs by tracing the algorithm.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Examination questions will involve specific algorithms in pseudocode or flow charts, and students may be expected to give an actual number or range of numbers of iterations that a step will execute.
coreConcepts: The number of times a step executes depends on the algorithm logic and the input values.
Tracing an algorithm precisely allows the iteration count to be determined.
Understanding iteration counts supports analysis of algorithm efficiency.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming a loop always runs exactly n times.
Forgetting to count the initial and final executions of loop conditions.
Ignoring conditional branches that affect how many times a step is reached.

conceptual: Determine the number of times the inner loop executes in a given nested loop algorithm.
Determine the number of comparisons made by bubble sort on an array of 5 elements.
examStyle: Determine the number of times the comparison step is executed in the following pseudocode for an input array of length 8. [6]
Determine the maximum number of comparisons needed to find a value in a sorted array of 128 elements using binary search.

topics.title: Introduction to programming
topics.syllabusDescription: Fundamental operations of computers, programming language features, variables, operators, loops, branching, collections and sub-programmes.

subtopics.title: State the fundamental operations of a computer
subtopics.assessmentStatement: State the fundamental operations of a computer.
subtopics.syllabusContent: State the fundamental operations a computer can perform: add, compare, retrieve and store data.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: These include: add, compare, retrieve and store data. Complex capabilities are composed of very large numbers of very simple operations.
coreConcepts: All complex computer operations are built from a small set of simple fundamental operations.
The four fundamental operations are: add, compare, retrieve and store data.
Understanding these operations reveals how software is ultimately executed in hardware.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming computers perform complex operations directly without breaking them down.
Confusing fundamental operations with high-level language statements.
Believing that retrieve and store are the same operation.

conceptual: State two fundamental operations of a computer.
State what fundamental operation is used to check whether two values are equal.
examStyle: State four fundamental operations of a computer. [4]
State the fundamental operation performed by a computer when it adds two values and stores the result in memory.

subtopics.title: Distinguish between fundamental and compound operations of a computer
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Distinguish between fundamental and compound operations of a computer.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Distinguish between simple fundamental operations and compound operations that are made up of multiple fundamental steps.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: For example, find the largest is a compound operation.
coreConcepts: Fundamental operations are the simplest actions a computer can perform.
Compound operations are composed of many fundamental operations.
Understanding this distinction supports algorithm design and analysis.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming that finding the maximum of two numbers is a fundamental operation.
Confusing compound operations with functions or sub-procedures.
Believing that compound operations cannot be broken down further.

conceptual: Distinguish between the fundamental operation of comparing two values and the compound operation of finding the largest of a list.
Explain why sorting a list is a compound rather than fundamental operation.
examStyle: Distinguish between a fundamental operation and a compound operation, giving one example of each. [4]
Explain why compound operations such as multiplication are built from fundamental operations at the machine level.

subtopics.title: Explain the essential features of a computer language
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Explain the essential features of a computer language.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Explain key features of programming languages including fixed vocabulary, unambiguous meaning, consistent grammar and syntax.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: For example, fixed vocabulary, unambiguous meaning, consistent grammar and syntax.
coreConcepts: A programming language has a fixed, well-defined vocabulary of keywords and symbols.
Syntax rules specify how valid programs must be structured.
Programs must be unambiguous so that computers can execute them deterministically.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming natural language ambiguity is acceptable in programming languages.
Confusing syntax errors with logical errors.
Believing all programming languages share the same syntax.

conceptual: Explain why a programming language must have unambiguous meaning.
Explain the role of syntax in a programming language.
examStyle: Explain three essential features that any programming language must have. [6]
Explain why a programming language must support both sequence and selection to be capable of solving general problems.

subtopics.title: Explain the need for higher level languages
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Explain the need for higher level languages.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Explain why higher level languages are needed to make programming more productive and to abstract from machine-level operations.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: As the human needs for computer systems have expanded it is necessary to abstract from the basic operations of the computer. It would take far too long to write the type of systems needed today in machine code.
coreConcepts: High-level languages allow programs to be written in a human-readable form.
Writing complex software in machine code would be impractically slow and error-prone.
High-level languages abstract away hardware details and improve portability.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming machine code is always faster than compiled high-level code.
Believing high-level languages hide all hardware considerations.
Confusing high-level languages with scripting languages only.

conceptual: Explain why modern software cannot realistically be written in machine code.
Explain two advantages of using a high-level language over assembly language.
examStyle: Explain the need for higher-level programming languages in the development of complex software systems. [6]
Describe two reasons why a programmer would choose to write a program in Python rather than assembly language.

subtopics.title: Outline the need for translation from higher level language to machine code
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Outline the need for a translation process from a higher level language to machine executable code.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Outline why translation is needed and describe translators such as compilers, interpreters and virtual machines.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: For example, compiler, interpreter, virtual machine.
coreConcepts: Computers can only execute machine code, so high-level programs must be translated.
A compiler translates an entire program before execution.
An interpreter translates and executes code line by line.
A virtual machine executes an intermediate bytecode representation.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing compilers with interpreters.
Assuming compiled code runs on any machine without modification.
Believing virtual machines are only used for running applications in a different OS.

conceptual: Outline the difference between a compiler and an interpreter.
Outline why a translation process is necessary before a high-level program can be executed.
examStyle: Outline the need for a translation process from a high-level programming language to machine code. [4]
Distinguish between compilation and interpretation as translation methods and state one advantage of each.

subtopics.title: Define the terms: variable, constant, operator, object
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Define the terms: variable, constant, operator, object.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Define variable, constant, operator and object in the context of programming.
coreConcepts: A variable is a named storage location whose value can change during execution.
A constant is a named value that does not change during execution.
An operator performs an operation on one or more operands.
An object is an instance of a class, combining data and behaviour.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing variables with constants.
Thinking operators are only arithmetic.
Assuming all objects are visible UI elements.

conceptual: Define the term variable.
Define the term constant and explain when it should be used instead of a variable.
examStyle: Define the terms variable and constant and state one difference between them. [3]
Explain the difference between a variable and an object, giving one example of each in the context of an object-oriented program.

subtopics.title: Define the operators =, ≠, <, <=, >, >=, mod, div
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Define the operators =, ≠, <, <=, >, >=, mod, div.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Define comparison and arithmetic operators including equality, inequality, relational operators, modulo and integer division.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Linked to approved notation sheet.
coreConcepts: Comparison operators return a Boolean result used in conditionals.
mod returns the remainder of integer division.
div returns the integer quotient of division without the remainder.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing = (assignment) with = (comparison) in pseudocode contexts.
Assuming mod and div always work the same way for negative numbers.
Confusing <= with < or >= with >.

conceptual: Define the operator mod and give an example of its use.
Define the operator div and show how it differs from standard division.
examStyle: Define the operators mod and div and give one example of each. [4]
Explain the difference between the div and mod operators and describe a practical situation where each would be used.

subtopics.title: Analyse the use of variables, constants and operators in algorithms
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Analyse the use of variables, constants and operators in algorithms.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Analyse how variables, constants and operators are used in algorithms and justify their use in specific situations.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: For example, identify and justify the use of a constant as opposed to a variable in a given situation.
coreConcepts: Variables store intermediate results and inputs that may change.
Constants are used for values that should not change, such as PI or tax rates.
Using constants instead of magic numbers improves readability and maintainability.
commonMisconceptions: Using variables for values that should remain constant.
Assuming constants are unnecessary in small programs.
Ignoring operator precedence when analysing expressions.

conceptual: Analyse an algorithm that calculates sales tax and justify where constants should be used.
Analyse the use of variables in a loop that accumulates a running total.
examStyle: Analyse the following algorithm and identify which values should be declared as constants rather than variables, justifying your answer. [6]
Construct pseudocode for an algorithm that uses variables and constants to calculate and output the area of a circle given its radius.

subtopics.title: Construct algorithms using loops and branching
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Construct algorithms using loops, branching.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Construct algorithms using loop and branching constructs from the approved notation sheet.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Teachers must ensure algorithms use the symbols from the approved notation sheet.
coreConcepts: Loops allow repetition of instructions for a set number of times or until a condition is met.
Branching uses conditions to select which block of code executes.
Combining loops and branching enables complex behaviour to be expressed in algorithms.
commonMisconceptions: Creating infinite loops by failing to update loop variables.
Using the wrong loop type for the situation.
Confusing the loop condition with the loop body.

conceptual: Construct an algorithm using a loop that outputs all multiples of 3 up to 30.
Construct an algorithm that uses branching to classify a grade as Pass or Fail.
examStyle: Construct pseudocode for an algorithm that reads 20 integers and counts how many are positive. [8]
Construct pseudocode for an algorithm that uses a loop and branching to output all even numbers between 1 and 50.

subtopics.title: Describe the characteristics and applications of a collection
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Describe the characteristics and applications of a collection.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Describe the characteristics of a collection and typical applications where collections are used.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Characteristics: contains similar elements. Collections are used to group related items so they can be processed together.
coreConcepts: A collection stores a group of similar elements that can be processed together.
Collections usually provide operations for adding, removing and accessing elements.
Using collections simplifies algorithms by abstracting how multiple elements are stored and traversed.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming a collection can only contain primitive data types.
Confusing collections with fixed-size arrays.
Believing all collections preserve insertion order or prevent duplicates.

conceptual: Describe one characteristic of a collection and give an example.
Describe how a collection could be used to store all bookings in a cinema reservation system.
examStyle: Describe the characteristics and one application of a collection in a school library system. [4]
Explain how using a collection instead of an array simplifies the management of a dynamic set of student records.

subtopics.title: Construct algorithms using the access methods of a collection
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Construct algorithms using the access methods of a collection.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Construct algorithms that use the standard access methods of a collection, such as adding items, checking for more items and retrieving the next item.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Algorithms should use access methods rather than indexing; for example, add(item), isEmpty, hasNext, getNext.
coreConcepts: Algorithms that use collections should work through defined access methods rather than assuming an internal representation.
Typical access methods include adding elements and iterating using operations like hasNext and getNext.
Using access methods supports abstraction and allows the underlying implementation of the collection to change without affecting algorithms.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming elements in a collection can always be accessed using numeric indexes.
Mixing array-style access with collection access methods in the same algorithm.
Forgetting to check termination conditions such as hasNext when iterating through a collection.

conceptual: Construct an algorithm using collection access methods to count how many items in a collection satisfy a given condition.
Construct an algorithm that searches a collection for a particular value using only its access methods.
examStyle: Construct pseudocode for an algorithm that uses the access methods of a collection to find the largest value it contains. [8]
Construct pseudocode for an algorithm that uses a collection to store a set of temperatures and outputs those above 37 degrees.

subtopics.title: Discuss the need for sub-programmes and collections within programmed solutions
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Discuss the need for sub-programmes and collections within programmed solutions.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Discuss why sub-programmes and collections are needed in programmed solutions, with reference to reusable code, modularity and maintenance.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Show an understanding of the usefulness of reusable code and program organization for the individual programmer, team members and future maintenance.
coreConcepts: Sub-programmes support modularity by dividing a solution into smaller, reusable parts.
Collections provide a structured way to manage groups of related data items.
Using sub-programmes and collections improves readability, teamwork, testing and future maintenance of software.
commonMisconceptions: Believing that using sub-programmes always makes programs slower and should be avoided.
Assuming collections are only needed in very large programs.
Ignoring long-term maintenance when deciding how to structure code.

conceptual: Discuss two advantages of using sub-programmes when developing a large software system.
Discuss why collections are useful when processing a large number of similar records.
examStyle: Discuss the need for sub-programmes and collections in the design of a school management system. [8]
Explain why breaking a large program into sub-programmes makes it easier to test and maintain.

subtopics.title: Construct algorithms using pre-defined sub-programmes, one-dimensional arrays and/or collections
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Construct algorithms using pre-defined sub-programmes, one-dimensional arrays and/or collections.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Construct algorithms that make effective use of pre-defined sub-programmes and simple data structures such as one-dimensional arrays and collections.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students will be expected to write and analyse pseudocode that calls existing sub-programmes and uses one-dimensional arrays and collections.
coreConcepts: Pre-defined sub-programmes and library routines can be reused to avoid re-implementing common functionality.
One-dimensional arrays and collections store multiple items and can be passed to sub-programmes as parameters.
Constructing algorithms using existing sub-programmes and data structures encourages modular, efficient solutions.
commonMisconceptions: Re-implementing standard algorithms instead of using available library sub-programmes.
Assuming arrays and collections behave identically in all cases.
Ignoring the implications of using third-party code without understanding or testing it.

conceptual: Construct an algorithm that uses a pre-defined Sort sub-programme to sort an array and then searches it using a pre-defined Search sub-programme.
Construct an algorithm that passes a collection of temperatures to a sub-programme that returns the average temperature.
examStyle: Construct pseudocode for an algorithm that uses pre-defined sub-programmes and either a one-dimensional array or a collection to read, store and then output all values above the average. [10]
Construct pseudocode for an algorithm that uses a pre-defined sub-programme and a one-dimensional array to count and output how many values in the array are negative.

topics.title: Abstract data structures
topics.syllabusDescription: Recursive thinking, abstract data structures including arrays, stacks, queues, linked lists and binary trees, and their operations and applications.

subtopics.title: Identify a situation that requires the use of recursive thinking
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Identify a situation that requires the use of recursive thinking.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Identify problems whose solutions can naturally be expressed in terms of smaller versions of the same problem.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Suggested practical activity: snowflakes and fractals, towers of Hanoi.
coreConcepts: Recursive thinking involves solving a problem by breaking it into smaller instances of the same problem.
Every recursive solution must have a base case that stops further recursion.
Problems such as fractals and the Towers of Hanoi are naturally suited to recursive solutions.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming recursion is always more efficient than iteration.
Forgetting that every recursive function must have a base case.
Confusing recursive thinking with circular reasoning.

conceptual: Identify one situation from everyday life that can be solved using recursive thinking.
Identify why the Towers of Hanoi problem is suited to a recursive solution.
examStyle: Identify two characteristics of a problem that suggest a recursive solution would be appropriate. [4]
Explain why a recursive solution is naturally suited to traversing a binary tree and identify the base case.

subtopics.title: Identify recursive thinking in a specified problem solution
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Identify recursive thinking in a specified problem solution.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Identify where recursive thinking is present in a given algorithm or solution.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Linked to binary trees.
coreConcepts: A recursive solution calls itself with a simpler version of the original problem.
Identifying recursion requires recognising the self-referential call and the base case.
Binary tree traversal is a common context in which recursive thinking appears.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing a loop with recursion.
Assuming a function that calls another function is automatically recursive.
Ignoring the base case when identifying recursive thinking.

conceptual: Identify the recursive call and base case in a given pseudocode function that computes a factorial.
Identify where recursive thinking is used in a binary tree traversal algorithm.
examStyle: Identify the base case and the recursive call in the following pseudocode. [4]
Trace a recursive pseudocode algorithm for calculating Fibonacci numbers with input 6 and state the final output.

subtopics.title: Trace a recursive algorithm to express a solution to a problem
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Trace a recursive algorithm to express a solution to a problem.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Trace the execution of a recursive algorithm step by step and state the output produced.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students will be required to state the output of the recursive algorithm. For example, trees.
coreConcepts: Tracing a recursive algorithm means following each call and its return value in sequence.
The call stack records each recursive call and returns values when the base case is reached.
Tracing helps verify the correctness of a recursive algorithm.
commonMisconceptions: Forgetting to unwind the call stack when tracing recursive calls.
Losing track of the current state of variables at each recursive level.
Assuming recursive calls are processed in parallel.

conceptual: Trace the recursive algorithm for computing factorial(4) and state the output.
Trace a recursive tree traversal and state the order in which nodes are visited.
examStyle: Trace the following recursive pseudocode with input value 5 and state the output. [6]
Explain what happens to the call stack during the execution of a recursive algorithm and describe a consequence of excessive recursion depth.

subtopics.title: Describe the characteristics of a two-dimensional array
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Describe the characteristics of a two-dimensional array.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Describe the structure and characteristics of two-dimensional arrays including rows, columns and indexing.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Linked to one-dimensional arrays and basic algorithms.
coreConcepts: A two-dimensional array is organized as rows and columns, accessible by two indices.
Elements are accessed using a row index and a column index.
Two-dimensional arrays are useful for representing grids, tables and matrices.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing row and column indices when accessing elements.
Assuming two-dimensional arrays must be square.
Treating a two-dimensional array as two separate one-dimensional arrays.

conceptual: Describe how elements in a two-dimensional array are accessed.
Describe one application where a two-dimensional array would be appropriate.
examStyle: Describe the characteristics of a two-dimensional array and explain how an element is accessed. [4]
Explain how elements in a two-dimensional array are accessed using row and column indices, giving one example.

subtopics.title: Construct algorithms using two-dimensional arrays
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Construct algorithms using two-dimensional arrays.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Construct algorithms that store, retrieve and process data using two-dimensional arrays.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Linked to pseudocode notation sheet.
coreConcepts: Processing a two-dimensional array typically requires nested loops to iterate over rows and columns.
Algorithms must correctly manage both indices when accessing or modifying elements.
Two-dimensional arrays are used to represent data such as game boards, tables and images.
commonMisconceptions: Swapping row and column indices, leading to off-by-one or out-of-bounds errors.
Forgetting to initialise both dimensions of the array.
Assuming the same algorithm for one-dimensional arrays works unchanged for two-dimensional arrays.

conceptual: Construct an algorithm using a two-dimensional array to find the sum of each row.
Construct an algorithm that transposes a two-dimensional array.
examStyle: Construct pseudocode for an algorithm that searches a two-dimensional array for a given value and outputs its row and column position. [8]
Construct pseudocode for an algorithm that uses a two-dimensional array to store and total the weekly sales figures for 4 products over 5 days.

subtopics.title: Describe the characteristics and applications of a stack
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Describe the characteristics and applications of a stack.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Describe the LIFO characteristic of a stack and its typical applications such as recursive processing and managing return addresses.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Characteristics: last in, first out (LIFO). Examples of applications include running recursive processes and return memory addresses.
coreConcepts: A stack is a LIFO data structure where the last element added is the first to be removed.
The primary operations are push (add to top) and pop (remove from top).
Stacks are used in recursion, expression evaluation and managing return addresses in programs.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing stacks with queues.
Attempting to access elements other than the top of a stack.
Ignoring the isEmpty check before performing a pop operation.

conceptual: Describe the LIFO characteristic of a stack using a real-world example.
Describe two applications of a stack in a computer system.
examStyle: Describe the characteristics of a stack and explain one application of a stack in program execution. [6]
Construct pseudocode to simulate pushing and popping elements on a stack implemented as an array, including an overflow check.

subtopics.title: Construct algorithms using the access methods of a stack
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Construct algorithms using the access methods of a stack.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Construct algorithms using stack access methods: push, pop and isEmpty.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Access methods: push, pop, isEmpty.
coreConcepts: push adds an element to the top of the stack.
pop removes and returns the element at the top of the stack.
isEmpty must be checked before calling pop to avoid errors on an empty stack.
commonMisconceptions: Popping from an empty stack without checking isEmpty first.
Using index-based access on a stack instead of the defined access methods.
Assuming push and pop are the only operations needed without ever checking isEmpty.

conceptual: Construct an algorithm that uses a stack to reverse the elements of an array.
Construct an algorithm that uses push and pop to check whether a string is a palindrome.
examStyle: Construct pseudocode for an algorithm that uses a stack to evaluate whether a sequence of brackets is balanced. [8]
Explain how a stack can be used to convert an infix arithmetic expression to postfix (Reverse Polish Notation).

subtopics.title: Describe the characteristics and applications of a queue
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Describe the characteristics and applications of a queue.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Describe the FIFO characteristic of a queue, linear and circular implementations, and typical applications.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Characteristics: first in, first out (FIFO). Applications include print queues and modelling physical queues. Both linear and circular implementations are required.
coreConcepts: A queue is a FIFO data structure where elements are added at the rear and removed from the front.
A circular queue reuses empty spaces at the front of a fixed-size array.
Queues are used in print spooling, scheduling and simulating real-world queues.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing the front and rear of a queue.
Forgetting the distinction between linear and circular queue implementations.
Treating a queue like a stack by removing elements from the wrong end.

conceptual: Describe the FIFO characteristic of a queue with a real-world example.
Describe the difference between a linear queue and a circular queue.
examStyle: Describe the characteristics of a queue and explain why a circular queue is more efficient than a linear queue in fixed-size implementations. [6]
Describe one application of a queue in an operating system and explain why the queue's FIFO property makes it suitable.

subtopics.title: Construct algorithms using the access methods of a queue
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Construct algorithms using the access methods of a queue.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Construct algorithms using queue access methods: enqueue, dequeue and isEmpty.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Access methods: enqueue, dequeue, isEmpty.
coreConcepts: enqueue adds an element to the rear of the queue.
dequeue removes and returns the element at the front of the queue.
isEmpty must be checked before dequeue to avoid errors on an empty queue.
commonMisconceptions: Calling dequeue on an empty queue without checking isEmpty.
Confusing the order of enqueue and dequeue operations.
Using index-based access instead of defined queue access methods.

conceptual: Construct an algorithm using a queue to simulate a printer job spooler.
Construct an algorithm that transfers all elements from a queue into a stack.
examStyle: Construct pseudocode for an algorithm that uses a queue to serve customers in order of arrival. [8]
Construct pseudocode for an algorithm that uses a queue to process print jobs in order of submission.

subtopics.title: Explain the use of arrays as static stacks and queues
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Explain the use of arrays as static stacks and queues.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Explain how one-dimensional arrays can implement static stacks and queues, including push, pop, enqueue, dequeue and full/empty checks.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should be able to explain push and pop operations and test on empty/full stack. Students should be able to explain enqueue and dequeue operations and test on empty/full queue.
coreConcepts: A static stack implemented as an array uses a top pointer to track the current top element.
A static queue uses front and rear pointers to track the ends of the queue.
Both require checking for full and empty conditions before push/enqueue or pop/dequeue operations.
commonMisconceptions: Forgetting to update the top or rear pointer after each operation.
Failing to check for overflow when pushing onto a full static stack.
Confusing the pointer update logic for stacks and queues.

conceptual: Explain how an array of size 5 can be used to implement a static stack.
Explain the role of the front and rear pointers in an array-based queue.
examStyle: Explain how a one-dimensional array can be used to implement a static queue, including how enqueue and dequeue are performed. [8]
Explain the difference between a static stack and a dynamic stack, and describe one limitation of a static stack.

subtopics.title: Describe the features and characteristics of a dynamic data structure
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Describe the features and characteristics of a dynamic data structure.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Describe the characteristics of dynamic data structures, including the concepts of nodes and pointers.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should understand the concepts of nodes and pointer.
coreConcepts: Dynamic data structures can grow and shrink at runtime by allocating and deallocating memory.
A node stores data and one or more pointers to other nodes.
Pointers link nodes together, forming the structure of lists and trees.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming all data structures are fixed in size.
Confusing a pointer with the data it points to.
Believing dynamic structures are always less efficient than static ones.

conceptual: Describe two characteristics of a dynamic data structure.
Describe the role of a pointer in a dynamic data structure.
examStyle: Describe the features and characteristics of a dynamic data structure. [4]
Compare a dynamic data structure with a static data structure in terms of memory usage and flexibility.

subtopics.title: Describe how linked lists operate logically
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Describe how linked lists operate logically.
subtopics.syllabusContent: Describe the logical operation of linked lists, including how nodes are linked by pointers.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Linked to logical thinking.
coreConcepts: A linked list consists of nodes where each node holds data and a pointer to the next node.
The head pointer identifies the first node; the last node's pointer is null.
Elements are not stored contiguously in memory, unlike arrays.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming linked lists allow direct index-based access like arrays.
Forgetting that the null pointer marks the end of the list.
Confusing the node's data with its pointer.

conceptual: Describe how nodes in a singly linked list are connected.
Describe what happens to the pointers when a new node is added to the front of a linked list.
examStyle: Describe how a singly linked list operates logically, including the role of the head pointer and null pointer. [4]
Describe how a new node is added to the end of a singly linked list, including how pointers are updated.

subtopics.title: Sketch linked lists
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Sketch linked lists (single, double and circular).
subtopics.syllabusContent: Sketch diagrams of singly, doubly and circular linked lists showing the effects of adding, deleting, modifying and searching for data items.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Students should be able to sketch diagrams illustrating: adding a data item, deleting a specified data item, modifying data, searching for a given data item.
coreConcepts: A singly linked list has a single forward pointer in each node.
A doubly linked list has both forward and backward pointers in each node.
A circular linked list connects the last node back to the first node.
Adding and deleting nodes requires updating the relevant pointers carefully.
commonMisconceptions: Failing to update all relevant pointers when adding or deleting nodes.
Confusing the direction of pointers in doubly linked lists.
Forgetting to handle the head pointer when modifying the first node.

conceptual: Sketch a singly linked list before and after inserting a node between the second and third nodes.
Sketch a circular linked list and show how it differs from a singly linked list.
examStyle: Sketch a doubly linked list containing the values 10, 20, 30. Show the result of deleting the node containing 20. [6]
Sketch a circular linked list containing the values 5, 10, 15 and describe how traversal differs from a singly linked list.

subtopics.title: Describe how trees operate logically
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Describe how trees operate logically (both binary and non-binary).
subtopics.syllabusContent: Describe the logical structure and operation of binary and non-binary trees.
subtopics.syllabusGuidance: Linked to recursive thinking.
coreConcepts: A tree is a hierarchical data structure with a root node and subtrees of children.
In a binary tree, each node has at most two children: a left child and a right child.
Non-binary trees allow nodes to have more than two children.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing trees with linked lists.
Assuming all trees are binary.
Thinking the root is always at the bottom of a tree diagram.

conceptual: Describe the difference between a binary tree and a non-binary tree.
Describe how a binary search tree maintains its ordering property.
examStyle: Describe how a binary tree operates logically. [4]
Explain the difference between a binary tree and a non-binary tree and give one application of each.

subtopics.title: Define the terms: parent, left-child, right-child, subtree, root and leaf
subtopics.assessmentStatement: Define the terms: parent, left-child, right-child, subtree, root and leaf.
